<ruby>辛<rt>から</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>苦手<rt>にがて</rt></ruby>なので、このカレーは**<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べられない**。<br>*I'm no good with spicy food, so I can't eat this curry.*

おいしいけれど<ruby>量<rt>りょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くて、このカレーは**<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきれない**。<br>*It's delicious, but there's so much of it that I can't finish this curry.*

In the first sentence the speaker cannot eat one spoonful. In the second they have been eating happily and have simply run out of room. Notice that `きれない` presupposes the action is under way or possible - which is why it fits so naturally with a half-empty plate.

---

## ～きれない · ～きれない vs ～すぎる

> **Rule of thumb** - `すぎる` describes **the thing**: there is too much of it. `きれない` describes **the person**: they cannot get to the end of it.

<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>すぎる**。<br>*There's far too much homework today.*

<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>までに**やりきれない**。<br>*I won't get through today's homework by tonight.*

---

## ～きれない · ～きれない vs ～すぎる (cont.)

They are two views of the same problem and they combine constantly - the commonest frame in the whole pattern is `～すぎて～きれない`: <ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>すぎて<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきれない. Using both is not redundant; the first names the cause and the second the consequence.

---

## ～きれない · ～きれない vs ～きった

> **Rule of thumb** - these are the two halves of one pattern. `きった` = got through the whole lot. `きれない` = could not.

<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きなピザだったが、<ruby>三人<rt>さんにん</rt></ruby>で**<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきった**。<br>*It was a big pizza, but the three of us polished it off.*

<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きなピザで、<ruby>二人<rt>ふたり</rt></ruby>では**<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきれなかった**。<br>*It was a big pizza, and the two of us couldn't finish it.*

---

## ～きれない · ～きれない vs ～きった (cont.)

The asymmetry to remember is that the affirmative side normally uses the **plain** form <code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきる / <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきった</code>, not the potential <code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきれる</code>, while the negative side almost always uses the **potential** <code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきれない</code> rather than the plain <code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べきらない</code>. Both plain negatives exist, but they sound deliberate - "doesn't finish it" rather than "can't finish it".

---

## ～きれない · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる**きれない** → ✅ <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**きれない**<br>*The suffix goes on the ます-stem.*

- ❌ <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**きれられない** → ✅ <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**きれない**<br>*`きれない` is already the potential negative. Adding another potential ending doubles it.*

- ❌ この<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さくて**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みきれない**。 → ✅ この<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さくて**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>めない**。<br>*Small print is a problem of ability, not of quantity. `きれない` needs an amount to fall short of.*

- ❌ <ruby>数<rt>かぞ</rt></ruby>えきれない**の**<ruby>星<rt>ほし</rt></ruby> → ✅ <ruby>数<rt>かぞ</rt></ruby>えきれない**ほどの**<ruby>星<rt>ほし</rt></ruby><br>*`きれない` is a negative い-adjective form, so it modifies a noun directly（<ruby>数<rt>かぞ</rt></ruby>えきれない<ruby>星<rt>ほし</rt></ruby>）or through `ほどの`. It never takes a bare `の`.*

---

## ～きれない · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>のライブが**<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちきれる**! → ✅ <ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>のライブが**<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちきれない**!<br>*The excited "I can't wait!" is the negative. The affirmative would mean you are perfectly capable of waiting, which rather kills the mood.*

---

## ～きれない · Practice 1

**1.** パーティーの<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>すぎて、<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ____。

{reveal}
<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**きれなかった**。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>すぎて</code> names the cause and `きれない` names the consequence - the standard pairing. The past `きれなかった` is needed because the party is over.

---

## ～きれない · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>が<ruby>悪<rt>わる</rt></ruby>くて、<ruby>遠<rt>とお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>が（<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>めない・<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みきれない）。

{reveal}
<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>が<ruby>悪<rt>わる</rt></ruby>くて、<ruby>遠<rt>とお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>めない**。

{reveal}
Poor eyesight removes the ability altogether, which is the plain potential negative. `きれない` would claim that the text is too long to finish, and it says nothing about eyes.

---

## ～きれない · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I got so many messages that I couldn't reply to them all."

{reveal}
メッセージが<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>すぎて、<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>には**<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>しきれなかった**。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>する</code> is a する-verb, so the stem is <code><ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>し</code>. The sentence is about volume defeating you rather than about not knowing how to reply, which is precisely `きれない`.

---

## ～きれない · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: おみやげが<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くて、<ruby>一<rt>いっ</rt></ruby><ruby>回<rt>かい</rt></ruby>では<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちきれられませんでした。

{reveal}
✅ おみやげが<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くて、<ruby>一<rt>いっ</rt></ruby><ruby>回<rt>かい</rt></ruby>では<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ち**きれませんでした**。

{reveal}
`きれる` already carries the potential meaning, so `きれられる` stacks two potentials. The polite negative past is simply `きれませんでした`.

---

## ～きれない · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一日<rt>いちにち</rt></ruby>では<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>め**ない**。 (b) この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一日<rt>いちにち</rt></ruby>では<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み**きれない**。

{reveal}
(a) says reading it in a day is beyond you - which could be because it is long, but could equally be because it is in a language you do not have, or too difficult. The sentence does not say which.

{reveal}
(b) narrows it to volume. You can read the book perfectly well; there are just more pages than fit into a day. It implicitly grants that you would get through it given longer, which (a) does not.

---

# ～がたい

**Meaning** · hard to bring oneself to ～; almost impossible to ～

`～がたい` (from <ruby>難<rt>かた</rt></ruby>い, voiced to がたい as a suffix) marks a difficulty that lives in the **mind, not in the hands**. Something is hard to believe, hard to accept, hard to part with, hard to put into words. It is not about a task being physically awkward - for that Japanese has a different suffix entirely.

---

## ～がたい · Formation

`がたい` attaches to the **ます-stem** and produces an **い-adjective**: <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい → <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたかった → <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたく → no `だ`.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (ます-stem) | ます-stem + がたい | <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じます → <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい |
| する-verb | Noun + し + がたい | <ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>します → <ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しがたい |
| Before a noun | ～がたい + Noun | <ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れがたい<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby> |
| Past | ～がたかった | <ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>け<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れがたかった |
| Polite | ～がたいです | <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたいです |
| Adverbial | ～がたく | <ruby>捨<rt>す</rt></ruby>てがたく<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |

---

## ～がたい · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - this suffix is **not productive**. It attaches to a short list of verbs of thinking, feeling, saying and judging: <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じる・<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>する・<ruby>想像<rt>そうぞう</rt></ruby>する・<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れる・<ruby>捨<rt>す</rt></ruby>てる・<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う・<ruby>認<rt>みと</rt></ruby>める・<ruby>近寄<rt>ちかよ</rt></ruby>る・<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>かす・<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>る・<ruby>耐<rt>た</rt></ruby>える. Everyday physical verbs do not take it: ❌<code><ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けがたい</code>, ❌<code><ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>きがたい</code>, ❌<code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べがたい</code>. If you are unsure whether a combination exists, it almost certainly does not - use `にくい`.

---

## ～がたい · Examples

あの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい**。<br>*His story is hard to believe.*

<ruby>一年間<rt>いちねんかん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れがたい**<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby>になった。<br>*The year abroad turned into an experience I'll never forget.*

どちらの<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>も**<ruby>捨<rt>す</rt></ruby>てがたい**ので、もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えさせてください。<br>*Both proposals have something going for them, so let me think a bit longer.*

なぜ<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>があんな<ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をついたのか、どうしても**<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しがたい**。<br>*I really cannot understand why he told a lie like that.*

---

## ～がたい · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し**<ruby>近寄<rt>ちかよ</rt></ruby>りがたい**<ruby>雰囲気<rt>ふんいき</rt></ruby>があるが、<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>してみると<ruby>優<rt>やさ</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>だ。<br>*The manager comes across as a bit unapproachable, but he's kind once you talk to him.*

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>の<ruby>段階<rt>だんかい</rt></ruby>では、この<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>したとは**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いがたい**。<br>*At this stage it would be hard to call the project a success.*

<ruby>信頼<rt>しんらい</rt></ruby>できる<ruby>同僚<rt>どうりょう</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>得<rt>え</rt></ruby>がたい**<ruby>存在<rt>そんざい</rt></ruby>だと、<ruby>転職<rt>てんしょく</rt></ruby>して<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>づいた。<br>*It took changing jobs for me to see how rare a colleague you can trust really is.*

<ruby>数字<rt>すうじ</rt></ruby>がこれだけそろっているのだから、この<ruby>結論<rt>けつろん</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>かしがたい**だろう。<br>*With this many figures lined up, this conclusion is going to be hard to shift.*

---

## ～がたい · Nuance & register

`がたい` is **noticeably formal**. It belongs to written Japanese, prepared speech, news copy and careful argument. In everyday conversation the same idea comes out as <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じられない, ちょっとわからない, <ruby>捨<rt>す</rt></ruby>てるのはもったいない. Saying <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたいですね in a chat with a friend is not wrong, but it lands like "that strains credulity" in English - correct, and a little theatrical.

The kind of difficulty it names is **psychological or principled**. A conclusion that is <ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>かしがたい is not heavy; it is well supported. A person who is <ruby>近寄<rt>ちかよ</rt></ruby>りがたい is not physically distant; they are intimidating. Note that this is a comment on how they come across and not necessarily a criticism - <ruby>近寄<rt>ちかよ</rt></ruby>りがたい often shades into "commands respect".

---

## ～がたい · Nuance & register (cont.)

The suffix is also useful for **hedged negatives**, and this is where business Japanese likes it. <ruby>成功<rt>せいこう</rt></ruby>したとは<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いがたい means "I would not go so far as to call it a success" - a way of saying it failed without saying it failed. <ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>しがたい softens a refusal in the same way.

Two lexical footnotes. ありがたい ("grateful, welcome") comes from this suffix historically but is now simply a word, and it is not built the same way. And the reading voices: がたい, not かたい. <ruby>固<rt>かた</rt></ruby>い and <ruby>硬<rt>かた</rt></ruby>い are unrelated adjectives about hardness.

---

## ～がたい · ～がたい vs ～にくい

> **Rule of thumb** - `にくい` is **practical** difficulty and attaches to almost any verb. `がたい` is **psychological or moral** difficulty and attaches to a short fixed list. When in doubt, `にくい` is nearly always the right answer.

この<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さすぎて**<ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>きにくい**。<br>*These shoes are too small and hard to walk in.*

<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>のことは<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>には**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いがたい**。<br>*It's hard to bring myself to tell my family about the accident.*

---

## ～がたい · ～がたい vs ～にくい (cont.)

Where a verb takes both, the difference is exactly this. <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いにくい is awkward to pronounce or awkward to raise - a practical obstacle. <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いがたい is something you cannot in conscience assert. Likewise <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じにくい ("hard to credit, on the evidence") is milder than <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい ("beyond belief").

Register follows the same line: `にくい` is at home everywhere, `がたい` is formal. Learners producing ❌<code><ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>いがたいアプリ</code> for "an app that's hard to use" are picking the wrong suffix twice over - wrong kind of difficulty and wrong level of formality.

---

## ～がたい · ～がたい vs ～ようがない

> **Rule of thumb** - `がたい` says it is hard and you would rather not. `ようがない` says there is **no method at all**, so the question of willingness never arises.

<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>い<ruby>訳<rt>わけ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい**が、<ruby>証拠<rt>しょうこ</rt></ruby>もない。<br>*His excuse is hard to believe, though there's no evidence either way.*

<ruby>連絡先<rt>れんらくさき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らないので、<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせ**ようがない**。<br>*I don't have his contact details, so there's no way to let him know.*

The first speaker *could* believe the excuse and is declining to. The second speaker would happily make the call and cannot. That is why `がたい` combines naturally with `が` and けれど - it admits the other side - while `ようがない` tends to close a topic down.

---

## ～がたい · ～がたい vs ～られない

> **Rule of thumb** - `られない` reports that you **cannot**. `がたい` reports that it is **hard to**, leaving the possibility open.

そんな<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>、とても**<ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じられない**。<br>*I simply can't believe a story like that.*

<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>内容<rt>ないよう</rt></ruby>には、いくつか**<ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じがたい**<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>がある。<br>*There are several points in the report that are hard to credit.*

The first is an emotional reaction, spoken, and it slams the door. The second is an assessment, written, and it leaves room for the report to turn out right after all. Choosing `がたい` where `られない` was wanted makes you sound as though you are drafting a memo in the middle of an argument; choosing `られない` in a formal document sounds hot-headed.

---

## ～がたい · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じる**がたい** → ✅ <ruby>信<rt>しん</rt></ruby>じ**がたい**<br>*`がたい` attaches to the ます-stem.*

- ❌ <ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れがたい**だ** → ✅ <ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れがたい<br>*The result is an い-adjective. The polite form is <code><ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れがたいです</code>.*

- ❌ この<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>狭<rt>せま</rt></ruby>くて**<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>りがたい**。 → ✅ この<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>狭<rt>せま</rt></ruby>くて**<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>りにくい**。<br>*Physical awkwardness is `にくい`. `がたい` is for difficulty of the mind.*

- ❌ しんじ**かたい** → ✅ しんじ**がたい**<br>*The suffix voices. Unvoiced かたい belongs to <ruby>固<rt>かた</rt></ruby>い and <ruby>硬<rt>かた</rt></ruby>い, which mean "hard" in the physical sense.*

---

## ～がたい · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みがたい**。 → ✅ この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みにくい**。<br>*A character that is hard to make out is a practical problem, and <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みがたい</code> is not a combination Japanese uses.*

---

## ～がたい · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>三十年<rt>さんじゅうねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ると、あの<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れ____<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れ**がたい**<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れがたい</code> is one of the fixed combinations, and as an い-adjective it sits directly in front of the noun with no `の` and no `な`. It is warmer and more literary than <code><ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れられない</code>.

---

## ～がたい · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: この<ruby>説明書<rt>せつめいしょ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さくて（<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みにくい・<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みがたい）。

{reveal}
この<ruby>説明書<rt>せつめいしょ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>字<rt>じ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さくて**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みにくい**。

{reveal}
Small print is a practical obstacle, and practical obstacles take `にくい`. <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みがたい</code> is not used at all - the verb <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>む</code> is outside the small set that takes `がたい`.

---

## ～がたい · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "At this point it would be hard to say the plan has gone well."

{reveal}
<ruby>現時点<rt>げんじてん</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>がうまくいっているとは**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いがたい**。

{reveal}
The frame <code>～とは<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いがたい</code> is the standard formal way to reject a claim without flatly contradicting it, and it is exactly what the hedged English sentence calls for.

---

## ～がたい · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>は<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しがたいだと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>は<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しがたいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
`がたい` builds an い-adjective, and い-adjectives take no `だ` before <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code>. The `だ` in the wrong sentence is the same error as ❌<code><ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code>.

---

## ～がたい · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>近寄<rt>ちかよ</rt></ruby>りがたい**<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>だ。 (b) <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しかけにくい<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
(a) describes the impression the manager gives off - a certain distance or gravity that makes people hesitate. It is formal in tone and can shade into respect: an imposing person is often described this way.

{reveal}
(b) is a practical complaint from the speaker's side: it is awkward to start a conversation with him, perhaps because he is always busy or always frowning. It is the more everyday phrasing, and it is about the speaker's difficulty rather than about his aura.

---

# ～ようがない / ～ようもない

**Meaning** · there is no way of doing it; no method exists

`よう` here is <ruby>様<rt>よう</rt></ruby>, "manner, way of doing". `～ようがない` therefore says that the **means are missing**: not that you lack the skill, not that you are unwilling, but that there is nothing available to do it with. No address, so no way to send it. No pieces left, so no way to mend it.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Formation

`ようがない` attaches to the **ます-stem** and the result is an **い-adjective**, because it ends in `ない`.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (ます-stem) | ます-stem + ようがない | <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>します → <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない |
| する-verb | Noun + し + ようがない | <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>します → <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようがない |
| Emphatic variant | ます-stem + ようもない | <ruby>想像<rt>そうぞう</rt></ruby>しようもない |
| Polite | ～ようがありません | <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがありません |
| Past | ～ようがなかった | <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けようがなかった |
| て-form / joining | ～ようがなく(て) | <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きようがなくて<ruby>困<rt>こま</rt></ruby>った |
| Before a noun | ～ようがない + Noun | <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない<ruby>時計<rt>とけい</rt></ruby> |

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - `ようもない` is the same pattern with `も` in place of `が`, and the `も` adds "not even". It is a shade stronger and a shade more literary; everything else is identical. Do not confuse either with the **volitional** <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こう</code>, <code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べよう</code> - those come from a different base and cannot take this ending.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Examples

<ruby>住所<rt>じゅうしょ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からないので、<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>り**ようがない**。<br>*I don't know the address, so there's no way to send it.*

こんなに<ruby>壊<rt>こわ</rt></ruby>れていては、<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>し**ようがない**。<br>*Broken like this, there's no fixing it.*

<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby><ruby>番号<rt>ばんごう</rt></ruby>も<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らないから、<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>し**ようがない**。<br>*I don't even know his phone number, so there's no way to get in touch.*

<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きく<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いてあるので、<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>え**ようがない**。<br>*The name is written in big letters, so there's no way you can get it wrong.*

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>本人<rt>ほんにん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>してくれない<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>、こちらからは<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>け**ようがない**。<br>*As long as he won't talk to us, there's nothing we can do to help.*

<ruby>材料<rt>ざいりょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>もないのだから、<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り**ようがない**じゃないか。<br>*There aren't any ingredients, so how exactly am I supposed to make anything?*

あのときの<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ちは、<ruby>想像<rt>そうぞう</rt></ruby>し**ようもない**。<br>*I cannot even begin to imagine how she felt at the time.*

データがすべて<ruby>消<rt>き</rt></ruby>えてしまったので、<ruby>報告書<rt>ほうこくしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き**ようがなく**、<ruby>締<rt>し</rt></ruby>め<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>りを<ruby>延<rt>の</rt></ruby>ばしてもらった。<br>*All the data was wiped, so there was simply no way to write the report and I had the deadline pushed back.*

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Nuance & register

The feeling is **resignation without excuse-making**. Because the sentence claims that no method exists, it removes blame from everybody: <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない is not "I failed to fix it" but "it was not fixable". That makes the pattern useful for declining responsibility gracefully, and it also makes it a strong claim - if a method *did* exist, the sentence is simply untrue.

There is a mirror-image use that surprises learners: `ようがない` on a verb of error or failure produces a **guarantee**. <ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えようがない means "you couldn't get it wrong if you tried"; <ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けようがない, "there's no way we lose". The logic is the same - no method available - but the effect is confident rather than defeated.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Nuance & register (cont.)

Register is neutral, leaning slightly written for `ようもない`. The one thing that is *not* neutral is the contraction. <ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない has a spoken cousin しょうがない, and しょうがない is a contraction of しようがない - so the two patterns share a form. In practice, しょうがない has drifted away into a fixed phrase meaning "oh well, nothing to be done", and it is quite casual; if you mean specifically "there is no way to do it", say しようがない with the full vowel.

Note also that しょうがない<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby> means "hopeless case, incorrigible" - an affectionate insult, not a comment on methods.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · ～ようがない vs the potential negative

> **Rule of thumb** - `られない` says **I** can't. `ようがない` says **nobody** can, because there is nothing to do it with.

<ruby>道具<rt>どうぐ</rt></ruby>がないので、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>には**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>せない**。<br>*I haven't got the tools, so I can't fix it.*

<ruby>部品<rt>ぶひん</rt></ruby>がもう<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>られていないので、**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない**。<br>*The parts aren't made any more, so it simply can't be repaired.*

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · ～ようがない vs the potential negative (cont.)

In the first sentence, a repair shop could still do it. In the second, nobody can. This is why `ようがない` is the right choice when you want to close off the possibility entirely - and the wrong choice when the obstacle is personal. ❌<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しくて<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きようがない is a common learner error; being busy is your circumstance, not an absence of method, so it should be <ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しくて<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>けない.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · ～ようがない vs ～がたい

> **Rule of thumb** - `がたい` is **hard**; `ようがない` is **impossible**. `がたい` concedes that the thing could be done and says you can hardly bring yourself to; `ようがない` says the question does not arise.

<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しがたい**が、<ruby>一応<rt>いちおう</rt></ruby><ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いておこう。<br>*His explanation is hard to make sense of, but let's hear him out anyway.*

<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby><ruby>枚<rt>まい</rt></ruby>もなくては、**<ruby>理解<rt>りかい</rt></ruby>しようがない**。<br>*Without a single document to go on, there's no way to understand it.*

The give-away is what can follow. `がたい` sits comfortably before `が` or けれど, because there is another side. `ようがない` normally ends the matter.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · ～ようがない vs 仕方がない

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない</code> is about **accepting a situation**: it can't be helped. `ようがない` is about **an action having no method**: there's no way to do it.

<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>止<rt>と</rt></ruby>まってしまったのだから、**<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない**。<br>*The trains have stopped, so there's nothing for it.*

<ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>も<ruby>電波<rt>でんぱ</rt></ruby>もないので、<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>を<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べ**ようがない**。<br>*With no map and no signal, there's no way to look up the route.*

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · ～ようがない vs 仕方がない (cont.)

<code><ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない</code> stands alone as a comment on the whole state of affairs and attaches to nothing. `ようがない` must attach to a verb stem and names a specific action that cannot be carried out. They often appear in the same breath: <ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べようがないのだから、<ruby>仕方<rt>しかた</rt></ruby>がない.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す**ようがない** → ✅ <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>し**ようがない**<br>*The suffix takes the ます-stem.*

- ❌ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こう**がない** → ✅ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>き**ようがない**<br>*The volitional <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こう</code> is a different form entirely. `よう` here is the noun <ruby>様<rt>よう</rt></ruby>, and it follows the stem.*

- ❌ <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>する**ようがない** → ✅ <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>し**ようがない**<br>*With a する-verb, the stem is `し`.*

- ❌ <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない**だ** → ✅ <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない<br>*It ends in `ない`, so it is an い-adjective and takes no `だ`. Polite is <code><ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがありません</code>.*

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>くて<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>し**ようがない**。 → ✅ <ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>くて<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>**できない**。<br>*Being sleepy is a personal state, not a missing method. `ようがない` needs the means themselves to be absent.*

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Practice 1

**1.** メールアドレスも<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby><ruby>番号<rt>ばんごう</rt></ruby>も<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からないので、<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせ____。

{reveal}
<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせ**ようがない**。

{reveal}
Every possible channel is missing, so there is literally no method - which is what `ようがない` claims. Note the ます-stem <code><ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせ</code>, and that the whole thing behaves as an い-adjective.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>丁寧<rt>ていねい</rt></ruby>すぎるくらいなので、<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>を（<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えようがない・<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えがたい）。

{reveal}
<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えようがない**。

{reveal}
This is the confident use: the instructions are so thorough that no route to a mistake exists. <code><ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えがたい</code> is not a combination Japanese uses, and `がたい` would in any case only mean "hard to", not "impossible".

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "The shop has closed down, so there's no way to complain about it now."

{reveal}
<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>がなくなってしまったので、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>となっては<ruby>文句<rt>もんく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>い**ようがない**。

{reveal}
The shop's disappearance removes the means, not the speaker's ability - exactly the distinction the pattern draws. <code><ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いようがない</code> sits on the ます-stem of <code><ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う</code>.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がなくて、<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>しようがなかったです。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がなくて、<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>できませんでした。

{reveal}
Lack of time is a personal circumstance, so the potential negative is what is wanted. `ようがない` would claim that no channel for replying existed at all - which would be true if the phone were dead, but not merely because you were busy.

---

## ～ようがない / ～ようもない · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) この<ruby>時計<rt>とけい</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>せない**。 (b) この<ruby>時計<rt>とけい</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しようがない**。

{reveal}
(a) says the speaker cannot repair it. Somebody with more skill, better tools or the right parts might well be able to, and the sentence quietly invites you to take it somewhere else.

{reveal}
(b) closes that door. There is no method - the parts do not exist, or the damage is past any repair - so taking it elsewhere would be pointless. It is a statement about the watch rather than about the speaker.

---

# ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる

**Meaning** · four suffixes that bolt a direction, a partner, a second attempt or a habit onto a verb

Japanese builds a great deal of its vocabulary by welding a second verb onto the ます-stem of a first. These four are the ones an N3 learner meets constantly: <code>～<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code> sends the action **inward or deep**, <code>～<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う</code> makes it **mutual**, <code>～<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す</code> makes it a **second go**, and <code>～<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる</code> says you have **done it often enough to be comfortable**.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Formation

All four attach to the **ます-stem** and produce an ordinary verb. <ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む, <ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う and <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す are **う-verbs**; <ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる is a **る-verb**.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (ます-stem) - inward | ます-stem + <ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む | <ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>びます → <ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む |
| Verb (ます-stem) - deeply, at length | ます-stem + <ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む | <ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えます → <ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む |
| Verb (ます-stem) - mutually | ます-stem + <ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>します → <ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う |
| Verb (ます-stem) - do over | ます-stem + <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す | <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きます → <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す |
| Verb (ます-stem) - get used to doing | ます-stem + <ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる | <ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>います → <ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる |
| Usual shape of the last one | ～<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れて + いる | <ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れている |
| Noun instead of a stem | Noun + に + <ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる | <ruby>生活<rt>せいかつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる |

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - these are **word-formation**, not free grammar. Each combination is a separate item of vocabulary, and only some combinations exist: <ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む is a word, ❌<code><ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>り<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code> in the sense "run inward" mostly is not. <ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む is the least predictable of the four - <ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む means both "use for years" and "embezzle" - so treat new combinations as vocabulary to look up rather than forms to generate. <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す and <ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う are the two you can most safely build yourself.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Examples

この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えたので、**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>します**。<br>*I got this kanji wrong, so I'll write it again.*

クラスのみんなで**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った**。<br>*The whole class talked it over together.*

<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもが<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>たまりに**<ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んだ**。<br>*The child jumped into the puddle.*

この<ruby>道具<rt>どうぐ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>十年<rt>じゅうねん</rt></ruby><ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>っているので、すっかり**<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れて**いる。<br>*I've been using this tool for ten years, so it's completely second nature by now.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いて、しばらく**<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んで**いた。<br>*The manager heard the question and sat there thinking hard for a while.*

<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>をやめるかどうか、もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>**<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>して**みることにした。<br>*I decided to give the question of quitting the exchange programme another think.*

<ruby>困<rt>こま</rt></ruby>ったときに**<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>け<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>える**<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちが<ruby>近<rt>ちか</rt></ruby>くにいるのは、ありがたいことだ。<br>*It's a blessing to have friends nearby who can help each other out when things go wrong.*

<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>満員<rt>まんいん</rt></ruby><ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>にもだんだん**<ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>り<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れて**きて、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>では<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>める。<br>*I've gradually got used to Tokyo's packed trains, and these days I can even read on them.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>で<ruby>昔<rt>むかし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>友人<rt>ゆうじん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>い、<ruby>喫茶店<rt>きっさてん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>二<rt>に</rt></ruby><ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>も**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んで**しまった。<br>*I ran into an old friend at the station and ended up talking for two solid hours in a coffee shop.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Nuance & register

All four are ordinary, register-neutral vocabulary. Nothing about them is formal or casual; what varies is how freely you can invent new combinations.

<code>～<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す</code> is the most productive and the most useful for a learner. Almost any deliberate action can be redone: <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す, <ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す, <ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す, <ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す, やり<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す. It always implies the first attempt was unsatisfactory, which is why it does not work for pleasant repetition - you do not <ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>き<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す a song you love, you listen again.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Nuance & register (cont.)

<code>～<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う</code> requires **two or more parties acting on each other**. That is a real constraint: <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>け<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う needs both sides helping, and if only one person helps, it is plain <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>ける. This use produces a warm, cooperative tone, which is why <ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>い is the word for a proper discussion rather than an argument.

<code>～<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code> splits into a physical direction（<ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む, <ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>り<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む, <ruby>流<rt>なが</rt></ruby>れ<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む）and an intensity or duration sense（<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む, <ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む, <ruby>黙<rt>だま</rt></ruby>り<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む, <ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む）. The second group tends to suggest being absorbed to the point of losing track of the outside world.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Nuance & register (cont.)

<code>～<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる</code> almost always appears as **～<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れている** or **～<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れてくる**, because it names a state you have arrived at rather than an event. And keep it apart from its noun-taking twin: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>生活<rt>せいかつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる takes a noun and `に`; <ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>で<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる takes a stem.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · ～直す vs もう一度～する

> **Rule of thumb** - <code>もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby></code> is neutral repetition. <code>～<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す</code> says the first attempt was **wrong or inadequate** and this is the corrected version.

<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きな<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>なので、**もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>**<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>たい。<br>*It's a film I love, so I'd like to watch it again.*

<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>抜<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>けていたので、<ruby>申込書<rt>もうしこみしょ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>した**。<br>*The name was missing, so I filled the application form in again.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · ～直す vs もう一度～する (cont.)

Swap them and the meanings shift audibly. <ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby><ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す would mean watching it again to check something, or - in another sense - coming to think better of it. もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby><ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>く is simply writing a second copy, with no implication that the first was faulty.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · ～合う vs 一緒に～する

> **Rule of thumb** - <code>～<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う</code> means the action goes **between** the participants. <code><ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に</code> means they do it **side by side**, usually to something or someone else.

<ruby>三人<rt>さんにん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>運<rt>はこ</rt></ruby>んだ。<br>*The three of us carried the luggage together.*

<ruby>困<rt>こま</rt></ruby>っている<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を、みんなで**<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>け<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>おう**。<br>*Let's all help each other out when we're in trouble.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · ～合う vs 一緒に～する (cont.)

The luggage is a third party; nobody is carrying anybody. That is why ❌<code><ruby>運<rt>はこ</rt></ruby>び<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う</code> is odd. With <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>ける, the sentence only takes <ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う if the helping flows in both directions - <ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>ける would mean two people helping a third.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · ～込む vs ～出す

> **Rule of thumb** - as directional suffixes they are opposites: <code><ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code> points **in**, <code><ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す</code> points **out**. Note that <code><ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す</code> also has the unrelated "suddenly begin" sense you met at N4.

かばんから<ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した**。<br>*I took my wallet out of my bag.*

ポケットに<ruby>切符<rt>きっぷ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んだ**。<br>*I shoved the ticket into my pocket.*

The same verb takes both and the pair is worth memorising: <ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す ("dash out, leap out") against <ruby>飛<rt>と</rt></ruby>び<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む ("dive in").

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · ～込む vs ～出す (cont.)

The trap is that <code><ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す</code> has a second job - marking the sudden start of an action, as in <ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>き<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す - and that job has nothing to do with direction. Context tells them apart: <ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す is "break into a run", not "run outwards".

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>く**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す** → ✅ <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す**<br>*All four attach to the ます-stem.*

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>相談<rt>そうだん</rt></ruby>し**<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った**。 → ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>相談<rt>そうだん</rt></ruby>した。<br>*<code>～<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う</code> needs the action to run both ways. Consulting a teacher goes one way, so the plain verb is correct.*

- ❌ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>生活<rt>せいかつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>み**<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れた**。 → ✅ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>生活<rt>せいかつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れた。<br>*With a **noun**, use <code>に<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる</code>. The stem form needs a verb in front of it: <code>この<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>み<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れた</code>.*

- ❌ この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>をもう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>**<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>もう**。 → ✅ この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>をもう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>**<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>そう**。<br>*<code><ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code> is to brood, absorbed and silent. To rethink something is <code><ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す</code>.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ このパソコンは**<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる**。 → ✅ このパソコンは**<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れている**。<br>*The suffix names a state you have reached, so the ている form is what you almost always want.*

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby><ruby>文字<rt>もじ</rt></ruby><ruby>間違<rt>まちが</rt></ruby>えたので、はじめから<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き____。

{reveal}
はじめから<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>した**。

{reveal}
The first version was faulty, which is exactly what <code>～<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す</code> marks. <code><ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す</code> is an う-verb, so the past is <code><ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>した</code>.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>では<ruby>全員<rt>ぜんいん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby>を（<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>い<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った・<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った）。

{reveal}
<ruby>全員<rt>ぜんいん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>い<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った**。

{reveal}
Opinions were exchanged between the participants, which is the mutual sense. <code><ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った</code> would mean everyone said the same thing in unison, which is not what a meeting is.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I've got used to cooking for myself, so it doesn't bother me any more."

{reveal}
<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れた**ので、もう<ruby>苦<rt>く</rt></ruby>にならない。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる</code> takes the ます-stem because the thing you are used to is an **action**. Had the sentence been about being used to *life alone*, it would need the noun pattern <code><ruby>一人<rt>ひとり</rt></ruby><ruby>暮<rt>ぐ</rt></ruby>らしに<ruby>慣<rt>な</rt></ruby>れる</code>.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たので、いそいで<ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>した。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たので、いそいで<ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>り**<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んだ**。

{reveal}
Getting onto a train is movement **inward**, so the suffix is <code><ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code>. <code><ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す</code> exists but means "lean out" or "launch into a venture" - not boarding.

---

## ～込む・～合う・～直す・～慣れる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>黙<rt>だま</rt></ruby>って<ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ていた。 (b) <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>黙<rt>だま</rt></ruby>り<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んで**しまった。

{reveal}
(a) simply describes what he was doing: not speaking, eyes down. It is a neutral piece of stage direction and says nothing about why.

{reveal}
(b) says he shut down into silence and stayed there. The <code><ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む</code> supplies both depth and duration - he has gone somewhere inward - and `しまった` adds that this was not what anyone wanted. It is a much heavier silence than (a).

---

# N3 - Talking about a topic, and who it's for

- ～について
- ～に関する / ～に関して
- ～において / ～における
- ～に対して
- ～にとって
- ～として
- ～向き - facing
- ～向き - suited to

---

# N3 - Talking about a topic, and who it's for (cont.)

- ～向け

---

# ～について

**Meaning** · about; concerning - names the subject matter that the talking, writing, thinking or investigating is *about*

`について` marks the **topic of an activity**. Something is being said, asked, written, researched or thought - and `について` says what it is about. It does not say who it is aimed at, and it does not say whose point of view we are taking. Those are jobs for other members of this same `に` family, and keeping them apart is most of the work at N3.

---

## ～について · Formation

`について` is a compound: the particle `に` plus the て-form of `つく` ("attach to"). It behaves as a unit and attaches to a bare noun - never to a verb or an adjective.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun, before a verb | Noun + について + verb | <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>について<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す |
| Noun, modifying another noun | Noun + についての + Noun | <ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>についての<ruby>記事<rt>きじ</rt></ruby> |
| Noun, as topic | Noun + については | <ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>については<ruby>後<rt>あと</rt></ruby>で |
| Noun, as addition | Noun + についても | <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby> → <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>についても<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>える |
| Noun, formal / business | Noun + につきまして（は） | <ruby>日程<rt>にってい</rt></ruby> → <ruby>日程<rt>にってい</rt></ruby>につきましては |
| Question word | <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby> / どこ など + について | <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby> → <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>について<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きますか |

---

## ～について · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - the `の` in `についての` is not optional. `について` is adverbial: it can modify a verb on its own, but to hang it on a noun you have to convert it with `の`, exactly as you would with <code><ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>での<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby></code>.

---

## ～について · Examples

<ruby>地震<rt>じしん</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べています。<br>*I'm looking into earthquakes.*

その<ruby>件<rt>けん</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>があります。<br>*I have a question about that matter.*

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>進路<rt>しんろ</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>相談<rt>そうだん</rt></ruby>しました。<br>*I talked to my teacher about which path to take after school.*

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>祭<rt>まつ</rt></ruby>り**についての**<ruby>番組<rt>ばんぐみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>録画<rt>ろくが</rt></ruby>しておいた。<br>*I recorded a programme about Japanese festivals.*

---

## ～について · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>**については**、あとでまとめてメールで<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせます。<br>*As for the cost of the trip, I'll send you the whole thing by email later.*

<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>**について**、<ruby>社員<rt>しゃいん</rt></ruby>からいくつも<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ている。<br>*Staff have raised a number of points about the new rules.*

その<ruby>画家<rt>がか</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>も<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らないまま<ruby>展覧会<rt>てんらんかい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>っても、たぶん<ruby>楽<rt>たの</rt></ruby>しめないだろう。<br>*If I go to the exhibition knowing nothing about the painter, I probably won't enjoy it.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あす</rt></ruby>の<ruby>説明会<rt>せつめいかい</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>来年度<rt>らいねんど</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>**につきまして**ご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>いたします。<br>*At tomorrow's briefing I will go over next year's budget.*

---

## ～について · Nuance & register

`について` sits in the middle of the register scale, and that is why it is the one to learn first. It is at home in a polite conversation, an email, a report, a university seminar and a news broadcast alike. Nothing about it is stiff; nothing about it is casual either.

Casual speech mostly does without it. Friends say <code><ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>のこと</code>, <code>あの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>のこと</code>, or just `～って`:

- あの<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>のこと、どう<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った? - "What did you think about that film?"
- <ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>って、いつだっけ。 - "The exam - when was it again?"

---

## ～について · Nuance & register (cont.)

Using について there is not wrong, but it lifts the sentence a register: it sounds like you are opening an agenda item rather than chatting. Conversely, an email to a client that says <code><ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>のことですが</code> where it could have said <code><ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>につきましては</code> reads as slightly under-dressed.

The `につきまして` form is worth recognising even if you never produce it. It is the same word with a humble-polite `ます` stem inserted, and it belongs to shop announcements, customer service and business correspondence: <code><ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>営業<rt>えいぎょう</rt></ruby><ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>につきましては…</code>. In ordinary polite speech it would sound over-formal, almost parodic.

---

## ～について · Nuance & register (cont.)

One structural habit to build: `について` likes to be followed by a verb of **speaking, writing or finding out** - <code><ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す</code>, <code><ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>く</code>, <code><ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する</code>, <code><ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べる</code>, <code><ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>える</code>, <code><ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>する</code>, <code><ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>する</code>, <code><ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>する</code>. If the predicate is an emotion or an evaluation instead, `について` is usually the wrong tool.

---

## ～について · ～について vs ～に関して

> **Rule of thumb** - same meaning, different register and different width. `について` points at a **specific** topic and is fine in speech; <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> is more formal, mostly written, and takes in the **surrounding area** of a topic as well.

You can swap them in most sentences without producing anything ungrammatical. What changes is how the sentence sounds, and how tightly the topic is drawn.

この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いた。<br>*I asked the teacher about how this kanji is read.*

---

## ～について · ～について vs ～に関して (cont.)

<ruby>外国人<rt>がいこくじん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>け<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れに**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**、<ruby>市<rt>し</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>方針<rt>ほうしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>示<rt>しめ</rt></ruby>した。<br>*The city has set out a new policy on accepting foreign residents.*

The first is one narrow question, asked out loud - `について` fits. The second covers a whole policy area, in writing, in a public register - <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> fits. Reverse them and neither is wrong, but the first would sound like a committee paper and the second like small talk.

---

## ～について · ～について vs ～に対して

> **Rule of thumb** - `について` is the **topic**; <code>に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して</code> is the **target**. "Talk about the customer" is `について`; "be polite to the customer" is <code>に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して</code>.

This is the pair that costs learners the most marks, because English "about" and "toward" both come out as "regarding" in a dictionary.

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新人<rt>しんじん</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>か<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていましたか。<br>*Did the manager say anything about the new hire?*

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新人<rt>しんじん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して**<ruby>厳<rt>きび</rt></ruby>しすぎると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う。<br>*I think the manager is too hard on the new hire.*

---

## ～について · ～について vs ～に対して (cont.)

In the first, the new hire is the subject matter of some remarks. In the second, the new hire is the person the manager's behaviour is aimed at. A useful test: if you can replace the phrase with "on the subject of", it is `について`. If you can replace it with "at / to / against", it is <code>に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して</code>.

---

## ～について · ～について vs ～のこと

> **Rule of thumb** - `のこと` is the everyday equivalent and, unlike `について`, it can be the **object of a feeling**. Verbs and adjectives of emotion take `のこと` (or a plain particle), never `について`.

<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>のこと**を**<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>しています。<br>*I'm worried about my little brother.*

<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>な<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>伝<rt>つた</rt></ruby>えました。<br>*I told the teacher the points about my brother that concern me.*

`について` needs the sentence to be *presenting information on a topic*. In the first sentence there is no presenting going on - there is only the feeling, and the brother is its object. The second sentence adds an act of communication, and `について` becomes available again.

---

## ～について · ～について vs ～のこと (cont.)

The same trap catches <code><ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>き</code>, <code><ruby>嫌<rt>きら</rt></ruby>い</code>, <code><ruby>怒<rt>おこ</rt></ruby>る</code> and <code><ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えている</code>. ❌<code>この<ruby>歌手<rt>かしゅ</rt></ruby>について<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです</code> is simply not Japanese; you want <code>この<ruby>歌手<rt>かしゅ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです</code>.

---

## ～について · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>について<ruby>記事<rt>きじ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んだ。（intending "an article about the accident"） → ✅ <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>**についての**<ruby>記事<rt>きじ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んだ。<br>*Without `の`, `について` modifies the verb <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んだ</code>, which gives "I read an article, about the accident" - a different and odd sentence. To attach it to a noun you need `についての`.*

- ❌ アニメについて<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。 → ✅ アニメ**が**<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。<br>*`について` introduces the subject matter of an act of communication or thought. A feeling takes its object with `が` or `を`, not with `について`.*

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>についてこの<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>**にとって**この<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>です。<br>*"For me, this job is important" is a standpoint, not a topic. Standpoints take `にとって`.*

---

## ～について · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby>について<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>な<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>った。 → ✅ <ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して**<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>な<ruby>態度<rt>たいど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>った。<br>*An attitude is directed *at* somebody. That is <code>に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して</code>; `について` would mean the rudeness was somehow on the topic of the customer.*

---

## ～について · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>工場<rt>こうじょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>移転<rt>いてん</rt></ruby>____<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
<ruby>工場<rt>こうじょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>移転<rt>いてん</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
The factory move is the subject matter of the discussion, and <code><ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う</code> is exactly the kind of communication verb `について` was built for. <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> would also be grammatical, just a notch more formal than a normal meeting warrants.

---

## ～について · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>店長<rt>てんちょう</rt></ruby>はアルバイトの<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>（について・に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して）とても<ruby>親切<rt>しんせつ</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
<ruby>店長<rt>てんちょう</rt></ruby>はアルバイトの<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>**に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して**とても<ruby>親切<rt>しんせつ</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>親切<rt>しんせつ</rt></ruby>だ</code> describes how the manager behaves **toward** somebody, so the students are the target of an attitude, not a topic of conversation. Say `について` and the sentence would try to mean that he is kind on the subject of part-timers, which is nonsense.

---

## ～について · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I'd like to hear your opinion about the new plan."

{reveal}
<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>**について**ご<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>いたいのですが。

{reveal}
<code>ご<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby></code> is information being given on a topic, so `について` is the natural choice. In a written request you could raise the register with <code><ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>につきましては</code>, and in casual speech you would drop the whole thing: <code><ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>、どう<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う?</code>

---

## ～について · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>についてのレポートを<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>してください。それから、<ruby>締<rt>し</rt></ruby>め<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>りについて<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>け<ruby>付<rt>つ</rt></ruby>けません。

{reveal}
✅ …<ruby>締<rt>し</rt></ruby>め<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>り**についての**<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>け<ruby>付<rt>つ</rt></ruby>けません。

{reveal}
The first `について` is correct because it already carries `の` before the noun `レポート`. The second one sits directly in front of the noun <code><ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby></code> and needs the same `の`. This is the single most common slip with this pattern.

---

## ～について · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さん**について**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しました。 (b) <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さん**と**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しました。

{reveal}
(a) makes <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さん the **subject matter**: somebody discussed him, and he may well not have been in the room. Depending on the context it can sound slightly ominous, in the same way English "we talked about you" does.

{reveal}
(b) makes him the **conversation partner** - you and he talked, about anything at all. `と` marks the person you do something jointly with; `について` marks what the doing is on the topic of. The two can even be stacked: <code><ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんと<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんについて<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しました</code> - "I talked with Yamada about Tanaka."

---

# ～に関する / ～に関して

**Meaning** · concerning; relating to; in connection with - the formal, largely written cousin of について（かんする・かんして）

<code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> and <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> mark the subject matter of a statement, a document, a rule or a piece of research. They mean what `について` means, but they belong to a different register - reports, notices, contracts, academic writing, the news - and they draw the topic **wider**: not just the thing named, but everything connected to it.

The two forms are one word doing two jobs. <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> is the dictionary form of a verb, so it modifies **nouns**. <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> is its て-form, so it modifies **verbs**.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Formation

`に` + <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> ("to be connected to"). The noun in front takes `に`, never `を`.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun, modifying a noun | Noun + に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する + Noun | <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby> → <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby> |
| Noun, modifying a verb | Noun + に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して + verb | <ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す |
| Noun, as topic | Noun + に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しては | その<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby> → その<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しては |
| Noun, as addition | Noun + に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しても | <ruby>人数<rt>にんずう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>人数<rt>にんずう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しても |
| Noun, business / keigo | Noun + に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しまして（は） | <ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby> → <ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しましては |
| Noun, modifying a noun (rarer) | Noun + に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しての + Noun | <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しての<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby> |

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> before a noun, <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> before a verb. <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>するの</code> does not exist: the `の` you are reaching for is already built into the verb form.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Examples

これは<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>です。<br>*These are the safety rules.*

その<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**は、<ruby>後<rt>のち</rt></ruby>ほどお<ruby>答<rt>こた</rt></ruby>えします。<br>*I'll answer that point later.*

<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>何冊<rt>なんさつ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ってしまった。<br>*I've ended up buying any number of books on health.*

<ruby>料金<rt>りょうきん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**ご<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby>のある<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>受付<rt>うけつけ</rt></ruby>までお<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しください。<br>*If you have questions concerning the fees, please come to the reception desk.*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>気候<rt>きこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>変化<rt>へんか</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>世界中<rt>せかいじゅう</rt></ruby>で<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>められている。<br>*Research relating to climate change is being carried forward all over the world.*

この<ruby>事件<rt>じけん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**、<ruby>警察<rt>けいさつ</rt></ruby>はまだ<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>も<ruby>発表<rt>はっぴょう</rt></ruby>していない。<br>*The police have released nothing in connection with this incident.*

<ruby>給与<rt>きゅうよ</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**は<ruby>不満<rt>ふまん</rt></ruby>はないが、<ruby>残業<rt>ざんぎょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>さに**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**は<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>え<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>してほしい。<br>*I have no complaints where pay is concerned, but on the amount of overtime I'd like the company to think again.*

<ruby>個人<rt>こじん</rt></ruby><ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>扱<rt>あつか</rt></ruby>いに**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しまして**は、<ruby>当社<rt>とうしゃ</rt></ruby>のホームページをご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>ください。<br>*Regarding the handling of personal data, please see our website.*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Nuance & register

This is a **written** pattern first and a formal-spoken pattern second. Its natural homes are notices, headings, minutes, contracts, textbooks, news copy and the polished parts of a presentation. If you say it to a friend over coffee you will sound like you are reading from a slide.

A useful gauge: the more institutional the speaker, the more likely <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> is. A company says <code><ruby>停電<rt>ていでん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>してお<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせします</code>; a housemate says <code><ruby>停電<rt>ていでん</rt></ruby>のことなんだけど</code>. Both are correct in their own place, and swapping them is the mistake.

<code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しまして</code> raises it one more step, into customer-facing business Japanese. It is extremely common in announcements and service email, and you should expect to hear it far more often than you produce it.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Nuance & register (cont.)

There is also a **width** difference that survives the register difference. `について` picks out a topic; <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> draws a circle around it. <code><ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する<ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby></code> covers the typhoon, the train stoppages, the school closures and the shop opening hours - everything connected to it. <code><ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>についての<ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby></code> is more likely to be information about the typhoon itself. This is a tendency rather than a hard line, but it is why headings and document titles overwhelmingly prefer <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code>.

Finally, do not confuse the phrase with the noun <code><ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby></code>. <code><ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>がある</code> claims a real-world connection between two things; <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> merely announces a topic. <code>この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby></code> is "material on this problem"; <code>この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>と<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby>がある<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby></code> is "material that turns out to be connected to this problem."

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · ～に関して vs ～について

> **Rule of thumb** - same meaning, different clothes. `について` is the everyday form and works in speech; <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> is formal, mostly written, and covers a broader area around the topic.

Nearly every sentence accepts both. Choose by asking who is speaking and where.

<ruby>夏休<rt>なつやす</rt></ruby>みの<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>**について**<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>で<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>した。<br>*The family talked about plans for the summer holiday.*

<ruby>市<rt>し</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**、<ruby>議会<rt>ぎかい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>激<rt>はげ</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby>があった。<br>*There was a fierce debate in the assembly concerning the city budget.*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · ～に関して vs ～について (cont.)

Put <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> in the first sentence and the family sounds like a board of directors. Put `について` in the second and nothing breaks - it is simply one notch less formal than assembly minutes would be.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · ～に関する + Noun vs ～についての + Noun

> **Rule of thumb** - both attach a topic to a noun, but the shapes differ: <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> takes **no** `の`, `について` takes an obligatory one. Titles, headings and formal documents prefer <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code>.

<ruby>留学生<rt>りゅうがくせい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>まいに**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**アンケート<br>*A survey concerning housing for international students*

<ruby>留学生<rt>りゅうがくせい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>まい**についての**アンケート<br>*A survey about housing for international students*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · ～に関する + Noun vs ～についての + Noun (cont.)

The second is perfectly good Japanese and is what you would say out loud. The first is what would be printed at the top of the form. Note the ❌<code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>するの</code> error is impossible to make with `について`, and the ❌<code>について<ruby>質問<rt>しつもん</rt></ruby></code> error (dropping `の`) is impossible to make with <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> - the two patterns fail in opposite directions.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · ～に関して vs ～において

> **Rule of thumb** - <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> gives the **topic**; `において` gives the **setting** - the place, the era, the field or the situation in which something holds.

Both are formal, both translate as "in" or "regarding" at some point in a dictionary, and both appear in the same kind of document, so they blur together.

<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**、<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>された。<br>*A new proposal has been put forward concerning safety measures.*

<ruby>建設<rt>けんせつ</rt></ruby><ruby>現場<rt>げんば</rt></ruby>**において**、<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby><ruby>対策<rt>たいさく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>よりも<ruby>優先<rt>ゆうせん</rt></ruby>される。<br>*On construction sites, safety measures take priority over everything.*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · ～に関して vs ～において (cont.)

In the first, safety measures are what the proposal is *about*. In the second, the building site is *where* the rule applies. If the noun could be preceded by "on the subject of", it is <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code>; if it could be preceded by "in" or "at", it is `において`.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**の**<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby> → ✅ <ruby>環境<rt>かんきょう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby><br>*<code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> is already a verb in its noun-modifying form, so it attaches to the noun directly. The `の` belongs to `についての`, not here.*

- ❌ <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>報告書<rt>ほうこくしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてください。（intending "the report on the accident"） → ✅ <ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>報告書<rt>ほうこくしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてください。<br>*Before a noun you need <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code>. <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> would attach the topic to <code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せる</code> instead - "show me a report, on the subject of the accident."*

- ❌ ゆうべの<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>そうよ。 → ✅ ゆうべの<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>**のこと**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>そうよ。<br>*Not a grammar error - a register error. Casual invitations do not take formal written vocabulary; the sentence sounds like a parody of a manager.*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して、この<ruby>決定<rt>けってい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>残念<rt>ざんねん</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>**にとって**、この<ruby>決定<rt>けってい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>残念<rt>ざんねん</rt></ruby>です。<br>*"For me" as a standpoint is `にとって`. <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して</code> would make *you* the subject matter of the decision.*

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>社員<rt>しゃいん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>に____<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>った。

{reveal}
<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>った。

{reveal}
The topic is being hung on the noun <code><ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby></code>, so you need the noun-modifying form <code><ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する</code> - with no `の` after it. <code><ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>についての<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby></code> would also work and would sound slightly less official.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>場所<rt>ばしょ</rt></ruby>（に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して・において）は、また<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>します。

{reveal}
<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>場所<rt>ばしょ</rt></ruby>**に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>して**は、また<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>します。

{reveal}
The venue is the **subject matter** of the message you will send, not the place where the sending happens. `において` would have to mean "I will contact you at the meeting venue", which is not what the sentence is doing.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese, in the register of a company notice: "We are currently investigating the cause of the problem. We will inform you separately regarding compensation."

{reveal}
<ruby>現在<rt>げんざい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>原因<rt>げんいん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>しております。<ruby>補償<rt>ほしょう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しまして**は、<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby>にご<ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>いたします。

{reveal}
A public notice is exactly where <code>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>しまして</code> belongs, and the `は` after it marks compensation as a separate item being set aside for later. <code><ruby>補償<rt>ほしょう</rt></ruby>については</code> would be acceptable but slightly plainer than a formal apology notice usually goes.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>してのついて<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
Two patterns have been welded together. Pick one: <code><ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby>に<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby></code> or <code><ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby>についての<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby></code>. Both mean "the explanation of the new system"; the first is the one you would print on an agenda.

---

## ～に関する / ～に関して · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>地震<rt>じしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>関<rt>かん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby> (b) <ruby>地震<rt>じしん</rt></ruby>**についての**<ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby>

{reveal}
(a) is the phrase a broadcaster or a city website would use, and it takes in everything connected to the earthquake - the tremor itself, the damage, the trains, the evacuation centres. The topic is drawn as a **field**.

{reveal}
(b) is what you would say in conversation, and it points more narrowly at information **about the earthquake itself**: how big it was, where it struck. The difference is a tendency rather than a rule, but the register difference is real and reliable: (a) is written and institutional, (b) is spoken and ordinary.

---

# ～において / ～における

**Meaning** · in; at; on - the formal written stand-in for で, naming the place, time, situation or field in which something holds（において・における）

`において` sets the **stage**. It tells you where something happens, when it happens, or within what field or respect a statement is true. Everything it does, the particle `で` also does - but `で` is the everyday word and `において` is the one that appears in announcements, papers, contracts and ceremonies.

`における` is the same word in noun-modifying dress: <code><ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>において<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>う</code> ("carry out at the venue") but <code><ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>における<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby><ruby>事項<rt>じこう</rt></ruby></code> ("points to note at the venue").

---

## ～において / ～における · Formation

Attaches to a bare noun. The `に` is part of the pattern and is not replaceable.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun (place), modifying a verb | Noun + において | <ruby>本社<rt>ほんしゃ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>本社<rt>ほんしゃ</rt></ruby>において<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>う |
| Noun (time or era) | Noun + において | <ruby>明治<rt>めいじ</rt></ruby><ruby>時代<rt>じだい</rt></ruby> → <ruby>明治<rt>めいじ</rt></ruby><ruby>時代<rt>じだい</rt></ruby>において |
| Noun (field or respect) | Noun + において | <ruby>技術<rt>ぎじゅつ</rt></ruby><ruby>面<rt>めん</rt></ruby> → <ruby>技術<rt>ぎじゅつ</rt></ruby><ruby>面<rt>めん</rt></ruby>において |
| Noun, modifying a noun | Noun + における + Noun | <ruby>職場<rt>しょくば</rt></ruby> → <ruby>職場<rt>しょくば</rt></ruby>における<ruby>関係<rt>かんけい</rt></ruby> |
| Noun, as topic | Noun + においては | <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby> → <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>においては |
| Noun, as addition | Noun + においても | <ruby>海外<rt>かいがい</rt></ruby> → <ruby>海外<rt>かいがい</rt></ruby>においても |

---

## ～において / ～における · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - `においての` exists but is uncommon and slightly clumsy. Before a noun, reach for `における`. Before a verb or an adjective, `において`.

---

## ～において / ～における · Examples

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>本社<rt>ほんしゃ</rt></ruby>**において**<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われます。<br>*The meeting will be held at head office.*

この<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>**において**、<ruby>両者<rt>りょうしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一致<rt>いっち</rt></ruby>している。<br>*On this point, the two sides are in agreement.*

<ruby>大会<rt>たいかい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>七日<rt>なのか</rt></ruby>、<ruby>市民<rt>しみん</rt></ruby>ホール**において**<ruby>開催<rt>かいさい</rt></ruby>いたします。<br>*The tournament will be held on the seventh of next month at the civic hall.*

<ruby>江戸<rt>えど</rt></ruby><ruby>時代<rt>じだい</rt></ruby>**における**<ruby>町人<rt>ちょうにん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>暮<rt>く</rt></ruby>らしを<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べています。<br>*I'm researching the lives of townspeople in the Edo period.*

---

## ～において / ～における · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>医療<rt>いりょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>分野<rt>ぶんや</rt></ruby>**における**AIの<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>急速<rt>きゅうそく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>がっている。<br>*The use of AI in the field of medicine is spreading rapidly.*

<ruby>面接<rt>めんせつ</rt></ruby>**においては**、<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す<ruby>内容<rt>ないよう</rt></ruby>だけでなく<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>も<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>られている。<br>*In an interview it is not only what you say but how you say it that is being judged.*

<ruby>我<rt>わ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>国<rt>くに</rt></ruby>**においても**、<ruby>人口<rt>じんこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>減少<rt>げんしょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>深刻<rt>しんこく</rt></ruby>な<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>となりつつある。<br>*In our country too, the falling population is becoming a serious problem.*

<ruby>価格<rt>かかく</rt></ruby>**においては**<ruby>他社<rt>たしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>負<rt>ま</rt></ruby>けているが、<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>**においては**<ruby>自信<rt>じしん</rt></ruby>がある。<br>*We lose to our competitors on price, but where quality is concerned we are confident.*

---

## ～において / ～における · Nuance & register

This pattern is **formal and written**, with essentially no casual life at all. Notices, minutes, academic papers, legal text, ceremonial speech and the polished register of the news are its habitat. Saying ❌<code>コンビニにおいてパンを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>った</code> is not a grammar error - it is a tonal disaster, roughly like writing "I did procure bread at the convenience store."

Two practical consequences.

First, **`において` covers only some of what `で` covers**. `で` marks place, but also means ("with a knife"), cause ("because of a cold"), material, and limit ("within a week"). `において` inherits only the **place, time, situation and field** senses. There is no ❌<code>ナイフにおいて<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る</code>.

---

## ～において / ～における · Nuance & register (cont.)

Second, the "field or respect" sense is where `において` earns its keep, because `で` there can be ambiguous. <code>この<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>において</code> - "in this respect" - is crisper in formal prose than <code>この<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>で</code>, which could momentarily be read as a location.

`において` also carries a faint ceremonial weight when used of an event. A wedding invitation says <code>ホテルの<ruby>大<rt>だい</rt></ruby>ホールにおいて</code>; a text to a friend says `ホテルで`. The formality is doing real work in the first case - it signals that this is an occasion.

---

## ～において / ～における · Nuance & register (cont.)

One last thing worth noticing: `における` is a fixture of **titles**. <code><ruby>現代<rt>げんだい</rt></ruby><ruby>社会<rt>しゃかい</rt></ruby>における<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>役割<rt>やくわり</rt></ruby></code> is exactly the shape of an essay title, a chapter heading, a conference paper. If you are writing academic Japanese, this is a phrase you will use constantly.

---

## ～において / ～における · ～において vs ～で

> **Rule of thumb** - same meaning, different register, narrower coverage. `において` can replace the **place / time / situation / field** uses of `で` and nothing else, and only in formal writing or formal speech.

<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>**で**<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。<br>*The match was held in Osaka.*
