Learning *through an experience* is the collocation <code><ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して</code> is most at home in. <code>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて</code> is not wrong, but essays and self-introductions overwhelmingly use <code><ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して</code> in this frame.

---

## を通じて / を通して · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>工事<rt>こうじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一週間<rt>いっしゅうかん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われました。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>工事<rt>こうじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一週間<rt>いっしゅうかん</rt></ruby>**にわたって**<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われました。

{reveal}
The construction is a single event measured from one end of the week to the other, which is what `にわたって` does. <code>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて</code> would need a continuing *state* - 「<ruby>一週間<rt>いっしゅうかん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>通<rt>つう</rt></ruby>じて<ruby>天気<rt>てんき</rt></ruby>がよかった」 is fine.

---

## を通じて / を通して · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) テレビ**で**その<ruby>歌手<rt>かしゅ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>った。 (b) テレビ**を<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>して**その<ruby>歌手<rt>かしゅ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>った。

{reveal}
(a) is the ordinary way to say it: the television was where you happened to come across the singer. Plain, spoken, no comment on the process.

{reveal}
(b) makes the television a **medium** and quietly draws attention to it - you know the singer only as television presented them, not in person. It is the version you would write in an essay about how media shapes what we know, and in casual conversation it sounds a little heavy.

---

# を中心に

**Meaning** · with X at the centre of it; centring on X; mainly X

Read <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code>. The noun before it is the **core**, and everything else in the sentence is arranged around that core - physically, as a circle on a map; or in terms of weight, as the part of an activity that gets most of the attention.

---

## を中心に · Formation

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | Noun + を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に | <ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby> → <ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>がる |
| Noun (stiffer, written) | Noun + を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>として | <ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby> → <ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>として<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>まる |
| Noun (deliberate arrangement) | Noun + を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にして | <ruby>文法<rt>ぶんぽう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>文法<rt>ぶんぽう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にして<ruby>復習<rt>ふくしゅう</rt></ruby>する |
| Before a noun | Noun + を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とする／とした + Noun | <ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby> → <ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とする<ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>チーム |

> **Note** - <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> modifies a **verb**. To modify a noun you must switch to <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とする</code> or <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とした</code>; the two are interchangeable, and the `とした` form is slightly more common in advertising and headlines.

---

## を中心に · Examples

<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>まっています。<br>*The shops are clustered around the station.*

<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>練習<rt>れんしゅう</rt></ruby>しましょう。<br>*Let's make kanji the focus of today's practice.*

その<ruby>歌<rt>うた</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中学生<rt>ちゅうがくせい</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>人気<rt>にんき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>がった。<br>*The song caught on above all among junior-high students.*

<ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>九州<rt>きゅうしゅう</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きな<ruby>被害<rt>ひがい</rt></ruby>をもたらした。<br>*The typhoon did serious damage, Kyushu worst of all.*

---

## を中心に · Examples (cont.)

この<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>会話<rt>かいわ</rt></ruby>でよく<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>う<ruby>言葉<rt>ことば</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>として**<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>められている。<br>*This dictionary is built around the words that come up most in conversation.*

<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>来年度<rt>らいねんど</rt></ruby>の<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>し<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>です。<br>*At next week's meeting we plan to centre the discussion on next year's budget.*

<ruby>市役所<rt>しやくしょ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とする**<ruby>半径<rt>はんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>一<rt>いち</rt></ruby>キロの<ruby>中<rt>なか</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>三<rt>みっ</rt></ruby>つもある。<br>*There are no fewer than three hospitals within a one-kilometre radius of the city hall.*

この<ruby>地域<rt>ちいき</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>昔<rt>むかし</rt></ruby>から<ruby>米<rt>こめ</rt></ruby>づくりを**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にして**<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>びとの<ruby>暮<rt>く</rt></ruby>らしが<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>いてきた。<br>*In this area life has long been organised around growing rice.*

---

## を中心に · Nuance & register

The pattern is at home in **written and semi-formal** Japanese - reports, weather bulletins, class plans, meeting agendas - but unlike many N3 noun patterns it is not stiff. 「<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>文法<rt>ぶんぽう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にやります」 is a perfectly ordinary thing for a teacher to say out loud.

The three variants shade upward in formality: <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> is the plain one, <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にして</code> puts a little more weight on the arranging being deliberate, and <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>として</code> is the essay-and-report form. Nothing turns on the choice; use the first unless you are writing.

---

## を中心に · Nuance & register (cont.)

<code><ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby></code> is still an ordinary noun meaning "centre", so the literal reading never quite goes away. That is a feature: 「<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る」 genuinely pictures rain spreading outward from a point on the map, and weather forecasts use it exactly that way. When the noun is a group of people rather than a place, the picture becomes one of concentration - the thing is happening most intensely there and thinning out at the edges.

One consequence worth noticing: the pattern implies that **other things are also included**, just less prominently. If a course covers grammar and nothing else, 「<ruby>文法<rt>ぶんぽう</rt></ruby>**だけ**」 is the honest wording; <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> promises a core plus a periphery.

---

## を中心に · を中心に vs 主に

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>主<rt>おも</rt></ruby>に</code> is a plain adverb meaning "mostly". <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> takes the thing as its object and adds the picture of a core with other material arranged around it.

この<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>では**<ruby>主<rt>おも</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す<ruby>練習<rt>れんしゅう</rt></ruby>をします。<br>*In this class we mostly do speaking practice.*

この<ruby>授業<rt>じゅぎょう</rt></ruby>では<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>す<ruby>練習<rt>れんしゅう</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**、<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>き<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>りもやります。<br>*This class centres on speaking practice, with listening as well.*

The second sentence needs the rest of the field to exist; the first does not care. That is why <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> so often has a `も` clause after it.

---

## を中心に · を中心に vs をはじめ

> **Rule of thumb** - <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> ranks by **weight**: X is the biggest part. `をはじめ` ranks by **order of mention**: X is the first and most representative member of a group, and the group is then named.

<ruby>関東<rt>かんとう</rt></ruby><ruby>地方<rt>ちほう</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**、<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>吹<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>いている。<br>*Strong winds have been blowing since morning, centred on the Kanto region.*

<ruby>関東<rt>かんとう</rt></ruby><ruby>地方<rt>ちほう</rt></ruby>を**はじめ**、<ruby>全国<rt>ぜんこく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>地域<rt>ちいき</rt></ruby>で<ruby>風<rt>かぜ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>まっている。<br>*Winds are strengthening in many regions across the country, Kanto among the first of them.*

---

## を中心に · を中心に vs をはじめ (cont.)

The first sentence maps intensity; the second opens a list. Swapping them produces sentences that are grammatical and slightly beside the point.

---

## を中心に · を中心に vs をめぐって

> **Rule of thumb** - `をめぐって` means the thing is the **point at issue**, and it usually brings disagreement with it. <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> is neutral about whether anyone is arguing.

<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>を**めぐって**、<ruby>社内<rt>しゃない</rt></ruby>で<ruby>意見<rt>いけん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かれている。<br>*Opinion inside the company is split over the new rules.*

<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>規則<rt>きそく</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**、<ruby>一時間<rt>いちじかん</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>があった。<br>*There was about an hour of explanation, focused on the new rules.*

`をめぐって` implies parties pulling in different directions; if all you mean is that a topic took up most of the time, it is the wrong word.

---

## を中心に · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>文法<rt>ぶんぽう</rt></ruby>**に**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します。 → ✅ <ruby>文法<rt>ぶんぽう</rt></ruby>**を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>します。<br>*The particle is `を`. The core is treated as something you *take* as the centre, not somewhere you put yourself.*

- ❌ この<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大学生<rt>だいがくせい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>まりです。 → ✅ この<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大学生<rt>だいがくせい</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とした**<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>まりです。<br>*<code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> needs a verb to modify. In front of a noun the pattern must become <code><ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とした</code> or <code><ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とする</code>.*

- ❌ この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>両国<rt>りょうこく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>激<rt>はげ</rt></ruby>しく<ruby>対立<rt>たいりつ</rt></ruby>している。 → ✅ この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>を**めぐって**、<ruby>両国<rt>りょうこく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>激<rt>はげ</rt></ruby>しく<ruby>対立<rt>たいりつ</rt></ruby>している。<br>*A dispute is fought *over* something, not *around* it.*

---

## を中心に · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べています。<ruby>肉<rt>にく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>一切<rt>いっさい</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べません。 → ✅ <ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>**だけ**<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べています。<br>*<code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> promises that other things are in the picture too. If there is no periphery, the pattern contradicts the next sentence.*

---

## を中心に · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明日<rt>あす</rt></ruby>の<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>西日本<rt>にしにほん</rt></ruby>____<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>くなるでしょう。

{reveal}
<ruby>西日本<rt>にしにほん</rt></ruby>**を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>くなるでしょう。

{reveal}
Weather forecasts use this pattern constantly: the rain will be heaviest in western Japan and lighter elsewhere. The literal "centre on a map" picture is exactly what is wanted.

---

## を中心に · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>（を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に・をめぐって）<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。

{reveal}
<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>**を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。

{reveal}
Nobody is arguing - someone is explaining. `をめぐって` would suggest the plan was contested, which does not fit <code><ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby></code>. Save it for <code><ruby>議論<rt>ぎろん</rt></ruby></code>, <code><ruby>対立<rt>たいりつ</rt></ruby></code> and the like.

---

## を中心に · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "It's a small company built around three engineers."

{reveal}
<ruby>三人<rt>さんにん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>技術者<rt>ぎじゅつしゃ</rt></ruby>**を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とする**<ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さな<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby></code> is a noun, so the pattern has to take its noun-modifying shape. <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>とした</code> would be equally good here.

---

## を中心に · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: このイベントは<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもに<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にして<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>されました。

{reveal}
✅ このイベントは<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ども**を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>にして**<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>されました。

{reveal}
The particle must be `を`. The `に` in the pattern is already supplied by <code><ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> itself, and doubling it is a common slip because so many neighbouring N3 patterns begin with `に`.

---

## を中心に · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>今回<rt>こんかい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。 (b) <ruby>今回<rt>こんかい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>主<rt>おも</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>若者<rt>わかもの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>対<rt>たい</rt></ruby>して<ruby>行<rt>おこな</rt></ruby>われた。

{reveal}
Both say that most of the people surveyed were young. (a) adds shape: young people form the core of the sample and other age groups sit around the edges, so the reader expects to hear about those edges later.

{reveal}
(b) simply reports a proportion. It makes no promise that anyone else was included and no claim about how the sample was designed - it is the flatter, more purely statistical of the two.

---

# をはじめ / をはじめとする

**Meaning** · starting with X - X being the leading member of a group, with the rest following

Written ～を<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>め in kanji, though kana is now more usual. The pattern names one item as the **most prominent or most representative** of a set, and then goes on to talk about the set as a whole. It is a listing device, not a substitute for "for example": what follows it has to be the group X belongs to.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Formation

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun | Noun + をはじめ、… | <ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby> → <ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>をはじめ、<ruby>各地<rt>かくち</rt></ruby>から<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>まる |
| Noun (formal, written) | Noun + をはじめとして、… | <ruby>校長<rt>こうちょう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>校長<rt>こうちょう</rt></ruby>をはじめとして、<ruby>先生方<rt>せんせいがた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>並<rt>なら</rt></ruby>んだ |
| Before a noun | Noun + をはじめとする + Noun | <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>をはじめとする<ruby>大都市<rt>だいとし</rt></ruby> |
| Before a noun (alternative) | Noun + をはじめとした + Noun | パンダ → パンダをはじめとした<ruby>動物<rt>どうぶつ</rt></ruby>たち |

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - the clause after the pattern must state the wider group, usually with a quantity word: <ruby>全員<rt>ぜんいん</rt></ruby>, <ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの～, さまざまな～, ～など. A sentence that names the leading item and then never mentions the set feels cut off halfway.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Examples

<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**、<ruby>社員<rt>しゃいん</rt></ruby><ruby>全員<rt>ぜんいん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>式<rt>しき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ました。<br>*The whole staff attended the ceremony, the president included.*

パンダ**をはじめ**、この<ruby>動物園<rt>どうぶつえん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>珍<rt>めずら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>動物<rt>どうぶつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い。<br>*Starting with the pandas, this zoo has a lot of unusual animals.*

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>**をはじめとする**<ruby>大都市<rt>だいとし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>人口<rt>じんこう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>まっている。<br>*In Japan the population is concentrated in the big cities, Tokyo foremost among them.*

この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>では、<ruby>米<rt>こめ</rt></ruby>や<ruby>味噌<rt>みそ</rt></ruby>**をはじめとする**<ruby>地元<rt>じもと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>品<rt>しな</rt></ruby>を<ruby>売<rt>う</rt></ruby>っている。<br>*This shop sells local produce - rice and miso and much else besides.*

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby><ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>**をはじめとして**、お<ruby>世話<rt>せわ</rt></ruby>になった<ruby>方々<rt>かたがた</rt></ruby>に<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いた。<br>*I wrote to everyone who had looked after me, beginning with Tanaka-sensei.*

<ruby>夏休<rt>なつやす</rt></ruby>みには、<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>の<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**、<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもが<ruby>巻<rt>ま</rt></ruby>き<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>まれる<ruby>事故<rt>じこ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>える。<br>*Over the summer holidays, accidents involving children - drownings first of all - increase.*

<ruby>今回<rt>こんかい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>大会<rt>たいかい</rt></ruby>には、アジア<ruby>各国<rt>かっこく</rt></ruby>**をはじめとする**<ruby>三十<rt>さんじゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>国<rt>くに</rt></ruby>と<ruby>地域<rt>ちいき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>する。<br>*More than thirty countries and territories will take part in this tournament, the nations of Asia among the first of them.*

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Examples (cont.)

この<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>江戸<rt>えど</rt></ruby><ruby>時代<rt>じだい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>旅館<rt>りょかん</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**、<ruby>昔<rt>むかし</rt></ruby>のままの<ruby>建物<rt>たてもの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>数多<rt>かずおお</rt></ruby>く<ruby>残<rt>のこ</rt></ruby>っている<ruby>珍<rt>めずら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>場所<rt>ばしょ</rt></ruby>だ。<br>*This is an unusual town where a great many buildings survive unchanged from the past, an Edo-period inn above all.*

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Nuance & register

This is **formal, largely written** Japanese: guidebooks, news reports, company announcements, and the opening of speeches. It is not something you say about your evening. 「<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>はビールをはじめ、いろいろ<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>んだ」 sounds like a press release about a night out; 「ビールとか、いろいろ<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>んだ」 is what a person says.

It is especially common in **thanks and greetings**, where naming the highest- ranking person first and then sweeping in everyone else is a fixed courtesy: 「<ruby>会長<rt>かいちょう</rt></ruby>をはじめ、<ruby>皆様<rt>みなさま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>よりお<ruby>礼<rt>れい</rt></ruby><ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げます」. Getting the order right matters - the named person should genuinely be the most senior or the most representative, and putting a junior name there reads as a slight.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Nuance & register (cont.)

On the kanji: modern writing usually leaves it in kana. If you do write it, it is `始` (as in <code><ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>める</code>, "to begin"), never `初`. And keep it apart from <code><ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて</code>, "for the first time" - a different word that sounds almost the same and produces nonsense if it slips in here.

Of the four forms, `をはじめ` is the everyday one, `をはじめとして` the most formal, and `をはじめとする` / `をはじめとした` are what you use in front of a noun. There is no meaning difference between the last two.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · をはじめ vs など

> **Rule of thumb** - `など` only says the list is partial. `をはじめ` additionally **ranks**: the named item leads the group, and the group has to be stated afterwards.

<ruby>机<rt>つくえ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>には、ペンやノート**など**が<ruby>置<rt>お</rt></ruby>いてあった。<br>*There were pens, notebooks and so on lying on the desk.*

この<ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>には、<ruby>古<rt>ふる</rt></ruby>い<ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**、<ruby>貴重<rt>きちょう</rt></ruby>な<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>がそろっている。<br>*This library holds a full range of valuable materials, old maps above all.*

Nothing about the pens is special; the old maps are the library's pride. The two often appear together - 「Aをはじめ、B や C など」 - with `をはじめ` picking the headline item and `など` closing the list off.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · をはじめ vs を中心に

> **Rule of thumb** - `をはじめ` opens a **list**; <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> describes a **distribution**, with the named thing carrying the most weight and everything else thinning out around it.

<ruby>山<rt>やま</rt></ruby>の<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**、<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>のうちに<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>積<rt>つ</rt></ruby>もった。<br>*Snow settled overnight, most heavily up the mountain.*

<ruby>北<rt>きた</rt></ruby>の<ruby>地方<rt>ちほう</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**、<ruby>各地<rt>かくち</rt></ruby>で<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>積<rt>つ</rt></ruby>もった。<br>*Snow settled in various places, in the northern regions first of all.*

The first is a map with a hot spot. The second is a roll call. `をはじめ` needs the group to be countable in some sense; a gradient of intensity is <code><ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby></code>'s job.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · をはじめ vs 例えば

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>例<rt>たと</rt></ruby>えば</code> is an adverb that opens a clause and introduces an illustration. `をはじめ` is a postposition that sits on a noun inside the sentence, and it cannot stand on its own.

<ruby>果物<rt>くだもの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。**<ruby>例<rt>たと</rt></ruby>えば**、りんごやぶどうをよく<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>います。<br>*I like fruit - apples and grapes, for instance, are things I buy often.*

りんご**をはじめ**、<ruby>秋<rt>あき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>果物<rt>くだもの</rt></ruby>はどれも<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>くなってきた。<br>*Autumn fruit has all come down in price, apples first among them.*

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · をはじめ vs 例えば (cont.)

<code><ruby>例<rt>たと</rt></ruby>えば</code> picks a random illustration and makes no claim about importance. `をはじめ` claims the item is the leading one, and it needs the group in the same sentence. ❌「をはじめ、りんごが<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです」 is not a sentence.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Common mistakes

- ❌ ケーキ**をはじめて**、<ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>いものが<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。 → ✅ ケーキ**をはじめ**、<ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>いものが<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。<br>*<code><ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて</code> ("for the first time") is a different word. The pattern ends in はじめ, or in はじめとして.*

- ❌ <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>をはじめ<ruby>都市<rt>とし</rt></ruby>で<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がっている。 → ✅ <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>**をはじめとする**<ruby>都市<rt>とし</rt></ruby>で<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がっている。<br>*In front of a noun the pattern needs `とする` or `とした`. Without it the reader stumbles over which word <code><ruby>都市<rt>とし</rt></ruby></code> belongs to.*

- ❌ カレー**をはじめ**、パンも<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。 → ✅ カレー**をはじめ**、<ruby>辛<rt>から</rt></ruby>い<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。<br>*The named item has to be a member of the group that follows. Curry does not lead a list whose next entry is bread.*

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さん**をはじめ**、<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれました。 → ✅ <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さん**をはじめ**、<ruby>大勢<rt>おおぜい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれました。<br>*The group must actually appear. On its own the pattern leaves the sentence unfinished.*

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>校長<rt>こうちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>____、<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>先生方<rt>せんせいがた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>見送<rt>みおく</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくださった。

{reveal}
<ruby>校長<rt>こうちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**（or **をはじめとして**）、<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>先生方<rt>せんせいがた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>見送<rt>みおく</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくださった。

{reveal}
The principal is the most senior member of the group named in the second half, and the second half supplies exactly the wider set the pattern needs. The honorific verb makes `をはじめとして` equally at home here.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: この<ruby>地方<rt>ちほう</rt></ruby>は、りんご（をはじめ・を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に）<ruby>果物<rt>くだもの</rt></ruby>の<ruby>産地<rt>さんち</rt></ruby>として<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>られている。

{reveal}
りんご**をはじめ**、<ruby>果物<rt>くだもの</rt></ruby>の<ruby>産地<rt>さんち</rt></ruby>として<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>られている。

{reveal}
Apples are one member of the category "fruit", and the sentence goes on to name that category - a list, not a distribution. <code>を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に</code> would suggest apples dominate the output and other fruit trails off around them, which is a claim about proportions rather than about what the region is famous for.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "Many countries, China and India above all, are increasing their imports."

{reveal}
<ruby>中国<rt>ちゅうごく</rt></ruby>やインド**をはじめとする**<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>国<rt>くに</rt></ruby>が、<ruby>輸入<rt>ゆにゅう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>やしている。

{reveal}
Two items can share the leading position, joined with `や`. Because <code><ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>国<rt>くに</rt></ruby></code> is a noun being modified, the pattern takes the `とする` shape rather than the bare `をはじめ`.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: この<ruby>美術館<rt>びじゅつかん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby>な<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>をはじめ、あります。

{reveal}
✅ この<ruby>美術館<rt>びじゅつかん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>有名<rt>ゆうめい</rt></ruby>な<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>**をはじめ**、さまざまな<ruby>作品<rt>さくひん</rt></ruby>があります。

{reveal}
The pattern names the leading item and then owes you the group. Left as it was, the sentence promises a set and never delivers one. Anything that names the wider category - <code>さまざまな<ruby>作品<rt>さくひん</rt></ruby></code>, <code><ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>美術品<rt>びじゅつひん</rt></ruby></code> - repairs it.

---

## をはじめ / をはじめとする · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) この<ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>には、アジア**をはじめとする**<ruby>世界中<rt>せかいじゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>留学生<rt>りゅうがくせい</rt></ruby>がいる。 (b) この<ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>には、アジア**を<ruby>中心<rt>ちゅうしん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>世界中<rt>せかいじゅう</rt></ruby>から<ruby>留学生<rt>りゅうがくせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ている。

{reveal}
(a) presents Asia as the first entry on a list of origins. It says nothing about how many students come from where - only that Asia is the region you would name first.

{reveal}
(b) makes a quantitative claim: most of the students are Asian, and the numbers thin out as you move away from that core. If a reader wanted to know the shape of the student body, (b) is the sentence that answers them.

---

# をこめて

**Meaning** · with X poured into it - putting a feeling, a wish or physical force into what you make or do

Written ～を<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>めて when kanji is used. The verb <code><ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>める</code> means to pack something into a container, and that is the picture: you are packing a feeling into an object or an action. The English gloss "filled with" is a trap - this pattern is never about ordinary physical fullness.

---

## をこめて · Formation

The noun in front comes from a small, closed set: feelings, wishes, and force.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun (feeling) | Noun + をこめて + verb | <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>をこめて<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>る |
| Noun (wish, prayer) | Noun + をこめて + verb | <ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>い → <ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>いをこめて<ruby>贈<rt>おく</rt></ruby>る |
| Noun (physical force) | Noun + をこめて + verb | <ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby> → <ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>をこめて<ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>す |
| Longer feeling phrase | Noun + の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち + をこめて | <ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ちをこめて |
| Before a noun | Noun + をこめた + Noun | <ruby>愛情<rt>あいじょう</rt></ruby> → <ruby>愛情<rt>あいじょう</rt></ruby>をこめた<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby> |
| Passive | Noun + がこめられている | <ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い → <ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いがこめられている |

---

## をこめて · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - the nouns that work here are few enough to learn as a list: <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>, <ruby>愛<rt>あい</rt></ruby>, <ruby>愛情<rt>あいじょう</rt></ruby>, <ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>, <ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い, <ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>い, <ruby>祈<rt>いの</rt></ruby>り, <ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち, <ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>. If your noun is not an emotion, a wish or force, the pattern is almost certainly the wrong one.

---

## をこめて · Examples

<ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**ケーキを<ruby>焼<rt>や</rt></ruby>きました。<br>*I baked the cake with all my heart.*

<ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>**をこめて**<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いドアを<ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>した。<br>*I pushed the heavy door with all my strength.*

<ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち**をこめて**、<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>花<rt>はな</rt></ruby>を<ruby>渡<rt>わた</rt></ruby>した。<br>*We handed the teacher flowers as a token of our thanks.*

<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>愛情<rt>あいじょう</rt></ruby>**をこめて**お<ruby>弁当<rt>べんとう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってくれた。<br>*Every morning my mother made me a packed lunch with real love in it.*

---

## をこめて · Examples (cont.)

「<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>になってね」という<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>い**をこめて**、<ruby>折<rt>お</rt></ruby>り<ruby>鶴<rt>づる</rt></ruby>を<ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>けた。<br>*We sent origami cranes, carrying the wish that she'd get well soon.*

この<ruby>曲<rt>きょく</rt></ruby>には、<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>強<rt>つよ</rt></ruby>い<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い**がこめられて**いる。<br>*There is a powerful feeling packed into this piece of music.*

<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>する<ruby>先輩<rt>せんぱい</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>**をこめた**アルバムをみんなで<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った。<br>*We all made an album, full of our thanks, for the graduating seniors.*

<ruby>優勝<rt>ゆうしょう</rt></ruby>してほしいという<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>い**をこめて**、<ruby>応援席<rt>おうえんせき</rt></ruby>から<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>けた。<br>*Willing them to win, we kept up our shouting from the stands right to the end.*

---

## をこめて · Nuance & register

The pattern is **warm and slightly literary**. It belongs to gift-giving, cards, speeches, product labelling and song lyrics, and it always implies that the speaker took care. Said about your own work it can sound either sincere or a little self-congratulatory, which is why advertising loves it: 「<ruby>職人<rt>しょくにん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>をこめて<ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つずつ<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>りました」 is close to a cliché on Japanese packaging.

Two of the collocations behave differently from the rest. <code><ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>をこめて</code> is plain and physical with no emotional colour at all - gripping, pushing, swinging. And `～がこめられている`, the passive, is the form you use to talk about meaning already inside something: a name, a song, a tradition. 「この<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>には<ruby>親<rt>おや</rt></ruby>の<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>いがこめられている。」

---

## をこめて · Nuance & register (cont.)

In casual speech people mostly do not use it. To say a friend's cooking was made with care you would more likely say 「<ruby>丁寧<rt>ていねい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってあるね」. Where it does turn up in conversation is in fixed farewells and dedications - 「<ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>をこめて」 written at the bottom of a card, or announced before a performance.

Note finally that the verb after it has to be an act of **making, giving or doing**. There is nothing to pack a feeling into if the predicate is a state: ❌「<ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>をこめてうれしいです」 has no container.

---

## をこめて · をこめて vs ～でいっぱい・～だらけ

> **Rule of thumb** - the English "filled with" covers three unrelated Japanese patterns. `をこめて` is a **feeling put into an act**. Plain physical fullness is `でいっぱい`. Unpleasant covering is `だらけ`.

バケツは<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>**でいっぱい**だった。<br>*The bucket was full of water.*

<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもの<ruby>服<rt>ふく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>泥<rt>どろ</rt></ruby>**だらけ**になっていた。<br>*The child's clothes were covered in mud.*

<ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いた。<br>*I wrote the letter with everything I had.*

---

## をこめて · をこめて vs ～でいっぱい・～だらけ (cont.)

❌<code><ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>をこめたバケツ</code> is not a stylistic problem, it is meaningless - water is not a feeling, and a bucket is not something you make. `でいっぱい` also handles abstract fullness where no act is involved: <code><ruby>不安<rt>ふあん</rt></ruby>でいっぱいだ</code>, "I'm full of worry."

---

## をこめて · をこめて vs をもって

> **Rule of thumb** - `をもって` is formal "with / by means of". It states the manner or instrument of an official act. `をこめて` says an emotion went **into** what you produced.

<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>として、<ruby>誠意<rt>せいい</rt></ruby>**をもって**<ruby>対応<rt>たいおう</rt></ruby>してまいります。<br>*As a company, we will respond to this in good faith.*

<ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**、この<ruby>歌<rt>うた</rt></ruby>を<ruby>皆様<rt>みなさま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>贈<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ります。<br>*With our thanks, we dedicate this song to you all.*

`をもって` is business and legal register - <code><ruby>書面<rt>しょめん</rt></ruby>をもって</code>, <code><ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby>をもって</code> - and it never carries warmth. Swap the two and the first sentence becomes oddly emotional while the second turns bureaucratic.

---

## をこめて · 力をこめて vs 力を入れる

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>をこめる</code> is **physical force at a moment**. <code>～に<ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>を<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れる</code> is **effort and resources put into an area over time**.

バットに<ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>**をこめて**、<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>り<ruby>振<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>った。<br>*I put everything into the bat and swung as hard as I could.*

<ruby>市<rt>し</rt></ruby>は<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>から<ruby>子育<rt>こそだ</rt></ruby>て<ruby>支援<rt>しえん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>**を<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れて**いる。<br>*Since last year the city has been putting real effort into childcare support.*

The second is a policy, not a muscle. Note the particle too: `をこめる` takes the force as its object, while <code><ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>を<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れる</code> marks the field with `に`.

---

## をこめて · Common mistakes

- ❌ コップに<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>**をこめて**ください。 → ✅ コップに<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>**を<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れて**ください。<br>*Only feelings, wishes and force can be packed in. For putting an actual substance somewhere, the verb is <code><ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れる</code>.*

- ❌ <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**にこめて**<ruby>歌<rt>うた</rt></ruby>います。 → ✅ <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**<ruby>歌<rt>うた</rt></ruby>います。<br>*The particle is `を`. The feeling is what gets packed, not the place it goes.*

- ❌ <ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>をもらった。 → ✅ <ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>**をこめた**<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>をもらった。<br>*In front of a noun the pattern takes `た`. As written, the sentence says *you* poured the gratitude in while receiving the letter.*

---

## をこめて · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**この<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。 → ✅ <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>から この<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。<br>*A feeling needs something to be packed into - an act of making, giving or doing. For "from the bottom of my heart" plus a state, the phrase is <code><ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>から</code>.*

---

## をこめて · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>退職<rt>たいしょく</rt></ruby>する<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち____<ruby>花束<rt>はなたば</rt></ruby>を<ruby>渡<rt>わた</rt></ruby>した。

{reveal}
<ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち**をこめて**<ruby>花束<rt>はなたば</rt></ruby>を<ruby>渡<rt>わた</rt></ruby>した。

{reveal}
Handing over flowers is an act you can pack a feeling into, and <code><ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち</code> is one of the pattern's standard nouns. The longer <code>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ち</code> version is slightly warmer than a bare <code><ruby>感謝<rt>かんしゃ</rt></ruby>をこめて</code>.

---

## をこめて · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>制度<rt>せいど</rt></ruby>については、<ruby>書面<rt>しょめん</rt></ruby>（をこめて・をもって）お<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせいたします。

{reveal}
<ruby>書面<rt>しょめん</rt></ruby>**をもって**お<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らせいたします。

{reveal}
A document is an instrument, not an emotion, and the sentence is formal business Japanese. `をもって` is the pattern for the manner or means of an official act; `をこめて` would be nonsense here.

---

## をこめて · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "She sings every song as though she means every word of it."

{reveal}
<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>はどの<ruby>曲<rt>きょく</rt></ruby>も<ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**<ruby>歌<rt>うた</rt></ruby>う。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>をこめて</code> is the standard way to say that an action is performed with genuine feeling rather than mechanically. Singing is an act, so it gives the feeling somewhere to go.

---

## をこめて · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: この<ruby>人形<rt>にんぎょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いをこめている。

{reveal}
✅ この<ruby>人形<rt>にんぎょう</rt></ruby>**には**<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>い**がこめられている**。

{reveal}
The doll is not the one doing the packing. When you want to describe the feeling already sitting inside an object, use the passive `がこめられている` and mark the object with `には`. The active form would need the maker as its subject: 「<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いをこめた<ruby>人形<rt>にんぎょう</rt></ruby>」.

---

## をこめて · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>力<rt>ちから</rt></ruby>**をこめて**ロープを<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>いた。 (b) <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>**をこめて**ロープを<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>いた。

{reveal}
(a) is a description of muscles: the rope was pulled hard, and nothing at all is being said about the puller's feelings. This is the one collocation in the family that is purely physical.

{reveal}
(b) is strange as a plain report and would only work in something like a festival or a ceremony, where pulling the rope is a meaningful act - hauling a shrine float, ringing a temple bell. The pattern always asks "what is this feeling being packed into?", and an ordinary tug of a rope has no room for it.

---

# N3 - Useful adverbs and connectors

- だけど
- ところで
- つまり
- たとえば
- 確かに
- おそらく
- もしかしたら
- まるで

---

# N3 - Useful adverbs and connectors (cont.)

- なるべく
- めったに
- 決して～ない
- べつに～ない・べつに～じゃない
- ふと - a thought that arrives on its own
- ふと - without meaning to

---

# だけど

**Meaning** · but; however - the casual sentence-opening "but"

`だけど` opens a **new sentence** that pushes back on the one just said. It is the everyday spoken "however": friends use it constantly, and it is one of the few words you should deliberately leave outside a job interview.

---

## だけど · Usage

`だけど` stands at the head of a sentence, with a comma after it in writing, and the objection follows. It does not conjugate, take particles or attach to anything - it is a fixed one-word opener.

- 「<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>海<rt>うみ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>こうよ。」「だけど、<ruby>台風<rt>たいふう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るらしいよ。」

Historically it is the copula `だ` plus the clause-final `けど` you met at N5, and that history explains the one place learners reliably go wrong. After a **noun or な-adjective** the same string turns up *inside* a sentence, because the `だ` belongs to the first clause: <ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>だけど、もう<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>いている. After a **verb or い-adjective** there is no `だ` available, so it is plain `けど`: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いけど<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>いにくい - never ❌<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いだけど.

---

## だけど · Usage (cont.)

Sentence-initially, then, `だけど` is always available. Mid-sentence it is only available after a noun or な-adjective, and there it is really two words wearing one coat.

One more very common shape: `～んだけど`, which prefaces a request or a piece of news - ちょっと<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>きたいことがあるんだけど… - where the trailing `だけど` softens the approach rather than contradicting anything.

---

## だけど · Examples

<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>い。**だけど**、<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>らないと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う。<br>*It's cold today. But I don't think it'll snow.*

「もう<ruby>一杯<rt>いっぱい</rt></ruby>どう?」「**だけど**、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いんだよね。」<br>*"Another drink?" "But I've got an early start tomorrow."*

<ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby><ruby>習<rt>なら</rt></ruby>った。**だけど**、まだ<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>すのはこわい。<br>*I studied it for three years. But phone calls still terrify me.*

<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>は<ruby>狭<rt>せま</rt></ruby>いし、<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>からも<ruby>遠<rt>とお</rt></ruby>い。**だけど**、この<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>なら<ruby>文句<rt>もんく</rt></ruby>は<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>えない。<br>*The flat is cramped and far from the station. But at this rent I can't complain.*

---

## だけど · Nuance & register

Casual. `だけど` belongs to conversation with friends and family, to messages, and to relaxed writing such as blog posts. In a business email, an essay or anything said to a customer, use `ですが` or `しかし` instead. Roughly, the ladder runs `しかし` (formal, written) - `ですが` (polite) - `でも` (neutral casual) - `だけど` (casual) - `けど` (very casual, often trailing off).

Against `でも`, `だけど` tends to be the firmer of the two. `でも` can register a mild reservation; `だけど` picks up the previous statement and argues with it, so opening several sentences in a row with it comes across as combative.

`だけれど` and `だけれども` are the unshortened forms: a shade more careful and slightly bookish, and they lean older in speech. `だけどさ`, `だけどね` do the opposite, softening the pushback with a final particle. None of these are marked for gender.

---

## だけど · Nuance & register (cont.)

Note also that `だけど` is not a subordinating conjunction. It cannot join two clauses into one sentence the way `が` or `けど` do; it needs a full stop in front of it, or at least the pause that a full stop would represent.

---

## だけど · だけど vs でも

> **Rule of thumb** - same slot, same register, different force. `でも` raises a qualification; `だけど` contradicts.

「これ、おいしいね。」「**でも**、ちょっと<ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>すぎない?」<br>*"This is good." "Though - isn't it a bit too sweet?"*

「これ、おいしいね。」「**だけど**、<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>た?」<br>*"This is good." "But did you see the price?"*

Both are natural; the second sounds more like the start of an argument. When you are not sure which you want, `でも` is the safer default.

---

## だけど · だけど vs けど

> **Rule of thumb** - `だけど` begins a sentence; `けど` ends a clause. They are not interchangeable positions.

<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>はある**けど**、お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がない。<br>*I have the time, but not the money.*

<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>はある。**だけど**、お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がない。<br>*I have the time. But I don't have the money.*

---

## だけど · だけど vs けど (cont.)

The content is identical; the second version breaks it into two beats and lands harder. Sentence-initial `けど` alone does exist in very casual speech - 「けど、<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>でしょ」 - but `だけど` is the standard choice there.

---

## だけど · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がないだけど、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。 → ✅ <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない**けど**、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。<br>*A verb or い-adjective cannot be followed by `だ`. Only nouns and な-adjectives can carry the `だ` that makes `だけど`.*

- ❌ <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かですだけど → ✅ <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かです**けど**<br>*`です` is already the copula; adding `だ` on top of it doubles up. In polite speech the clause-final connector is `ですけど` or `ですが`.*

- ❌（<ruby>取引先<rt>とりひきさき</rt></ruby>へのメールで）だけど、<ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>になります。 → ✅ **しかし**、<ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>になります。<br>*`だけど` in business writing reads as though you forgot who you were talking to. `しかし` or `ですが` carries the same meaning at the right register.*

---

## だけど · Practice 1

**1.** 「<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>のパーティー、<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る?」「<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。____、バイトなんだ。」

{reveal}
「<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたい。**だけど**、バイトなんだ。」

{reveal}
The speaker has finished one sentence and starts another that contradicts it, so the connector has to be the sentence-initial kind. `でも` would also fit here and would sound a little softer.

---

## だけど · Practice 2

**2.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いだけど、けっきょく<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うことにした。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い**けど**、けっきょく<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うことにした。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い</code> is an い-adjective, and い-adjectives are never followed by `だ`. Splitting it into two sentences - <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。だけど、<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うことにした。 - works too.

---

## だけど · Practice 3

**3.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) **だけど**、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>はそうは<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>わない。 (b) **ですが**、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>はそうは<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いません。

{reveal}
The grammar is the same and the meaning is the same: both reject what was just said. The difference is entirely register. Sentence (a) is what you say to a friend over coffee, while (b) is what you say in a meeting or write in an essay. Using (a) in a formal discussion would sound abrupt and a little rude, and using (b) with a close friend would sound stiff and distant.

---

# ところで

**Meaning** · by the way - putting the current topic down and picking up a new one

`ところで` is a signal, not a link. It tells the listener that what follows has nothing to do with what came before, and that the speaker is doing it on purpose. Nine times out of ten, what follows is a question the speaker has been sitting on.

---

## ところで · Usage

`ところで` goes at the **head of a sentence**, followed by a comma or a pause. It does not attach to a word, does not conjugate, and never appears in the middle of a clause.

- ところで、<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>はどうなりましたか。
- ところで、あの<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>、<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えてる?

---

## ところで · Usage (cont.)

Two things it is *not*. It is not "however" - it contradicts nothing, so ❌ところで、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>です is wrong where `しかし` was wanted. And it is not the `ところ` family of grammar points: the `～たところで` of <ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>いだところで<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わない ("even if you hurry…") and the `～ているところ` of <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べているところです ("in the middle of eating") are separate constructions that merely look alike. The `ところで` of this page always begins a sentence and never follows a verb.

Because the whole point of the word is to close one subject and open another, it usually appears once in a conversation, at a natural seam - after a topic has run its course, not on top of someone else who is still talking.

---

## ところで · Examples

**ところで**、<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>?<br>*By the way, how's Yamada doing?*

**ところで**、<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんはもう<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べましたか。<br>*By the way, have you had lunch yet?*

<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>以上<rt>いじょう</rt></ruby>です。**ところで**、<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何時<rt>なんじ</rt></ruby>からでしたか。<br>*That's everything in the handouts. By the way, what time was next week's meeting again?*

<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>、ありがとう。すごくよく<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>れてるね。**ところで**、あのカメラっていくらぐらいしたの?<br>*Thanks for the photos - they came out really well. By the way, roughly how much was that camera?*

---

## ところで · Nuance & register

`ところで` is register-neutral in itself: it works in ます-form speech and in plain speech, and it appears in writing wherever a writer changes tack. What is not neutral is the act it performs. Announcing a change of subject is a small claim on the floor, so it lands most comfortably when you have the standing to make it - among equals, or from whoever is hosting the conversation.

Speaking to a customer or someone well above you, the same move is usually padded: <ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わりますが、… or それはそうと、… or simply <ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つお<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>いしてもよろしいでしょうか. `ところで` itself is not rude - it is used in business meetings constantly - but it is brisk, and dropped straight after someone has said something emotionally weighty it can sound as though you were not listening.

There is no casual contraction of it, and it is not marked for age or gender.

---

## ところで · ところで vs ちなみに

> **Rule of thumb** - `ところで` drops the current topic. `ちなみに` stays on it and adds a footnote.

このカフェ、<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>くておいしいよ。**ちなみに**、<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>は<ruby>十時<rt>じゅうじ</rt></ruby>までやってる。<br>*This café is cheap and good. Incidentally, it's open until ten at night.*

このカフェ、<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>くておいしいよ。**ところで**、<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しの<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby>は<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>んでる?<br>*This café is cheap and good. Anyway - how's the packing for your move coming along?*

Swapping them breaks both sentences: the opening hours are plainly still about the café, and the packing plainly is not. A quick test - if the new sentence would also work with そういえば in front of it, `ところで` is the right choice.

---

## ところで · Common mistakes

- ❌ ところで、この<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>できません。 → ✅ **しかし**、この<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>には<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>できません。<br>*`ところで` changes the subject; it does not disagree. Learners reach for it because it looks like a conjunction, but it carries no adversative meaning at all.*

- ❌ <ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>たところで、<ruby>晩<rt>ばん</rt></ruby>ごはんは<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>にする?（meaning "by the way"）→ ✅ <ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>、<ruby>面白<rt>おもしろ</rt></ruby>かったね。**ところで**、<ruby>晩<rt>ばん</rt></ruby>ごはんは<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>にする?<br>*Placed after a verb, the same syllables become the pattern meaning "even if", and the sentence turns into "even if I watch the film…". Keep it at the front.*

- ❌ ところでですが、… → ✅ ところで、…<br>*`ところで` already contains everything it needs, and `ですが` does not politen it. If you want a politer version, replace the whole word with <ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わりますが.*

---

## ところで · Practice 1

**1.** ____、<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんの<ruby>連絡先<rt>れんらくさき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っていますか。

{reveal}
**ところで**、<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんの<ruby>連絡先<rt>れんらくさき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っていますか。

{reveal}
A question with no connection to the previous topic needs a marker warning the listener to switch tracks, and that is exactly the job this word does.

---

## ところで · Practice 2

**2.** Choose the natural connector: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>市民<rt>しみん</rt></ruby>ホールです。（ところで・ちなみに）、<ruby>駐車場<rt>ちゅうしゃじょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>有料<rt>ゆうりょう</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
**ちなみに**、<ruby>駐車場<rt>ちゅうしゃじょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>有料<rt>ゆうりょう</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
The parking charge is a further detail about the same venue, so the topic has not changed at all. `ところで` would promise the listener something unrelated and then fail to deliver it.

---

## ところで · Practice 3

**3.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) ところで、<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、そろそろ<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>してもよろしいでしょうか。 (b) <ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わりますが、<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、そろそろ<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>してもよろしいでしょうか。

{reveal}
Both change the subject and both are grammatical. Sentence (a) is brisk: the speaker announces the switch in one word and moves on, which is fine between colleagues but a little bald when addressing a superior. Sentence (b) spends a few extra syllables acknowledging that a switch is being made, and that small detour is what makes it sound considerate.

---

# つまり

**Meaning** · in other words; which means - restating something more plainly, or spelling out what it amounts to

`つまり` announces that the same content is coming round again in a clearer shape. It does two jobs with one word: rewording something complicated, and stating the consequence nobody has said out loud yet.

---

## つまり · Usage

`つまり` is an adverb and sits at the front of the clause it introduces. Nothing attaches to it, and it never changes form.

The habit worth building is what comes at the **end** of that clause. A `つまり` sentence very often closes with `ということだ`, `わけだ` or `のだ`, because you are labelling a conclusion rather than reporting a fresh fact:

- つまり、<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>られないということですね。
- <ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby><ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいた。つまり、<ruby>地元<rt>じもと</rt></ruby>のようなものだ。

The two jobs, one line each:

---

## つまり · Usage (cont.)

- **Rewording** - the second half says the same thing in easier words.<br>*<ruby>検討<rt>けんとう</rt></ruby>します。つまり、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>は<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>められないということです。*
- **Consequence** - the second half is what the first one comes to.<br>*<ruby>終電<rt>しゅうでん</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た。つまり、<ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>いて<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るしかない。*

As a standalone check on your understanding, `つまり` with a rising question is extremely common: 「つまり、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みってこと?」

---

## つまり · Examples

<ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>の<ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>、**つまり**おばです。<br>*My father's older sister - my aunt, in other words.*

<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>がない。**つまり**、<ruby>断<rt>ことわ</rt></ruby>られたということだ。<br>*There's been no reply. Which means I've been turned down.*

<ruby>材料費<rt>ざいりょうひ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>送料<rt>そうりょう</rt></ruby>も<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がっている。**つまり**、<ruby>値上<rt>ねあ</rt></ruby>げは<ruby>避<rt>さ</rt></ruby>けられないわけです。<br>*Materials and shipping have both gone up. In other words, a price rise can't be avoided.*

「<ruby>前向<rt>まえむ</rt></ruby>きに<ruby>検討<rt>けんとう</rt></ruby>します」って<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われたんだけど、**つまり**<ruby>断<rt>ことわ</rt></ruby>られたってこと?<br>*They said they'd "consider it positively" - so does that mean I've been refused?*

---

## つまり · Nuance & register

Register-neutral and very frequent. It is at home in a lecture, a contract summary, a news broadcast and a conversation between friends, with no change of form.

In speech it has a second life as a filler. Some speakers open every third sentence with つまり、つまりですね… while they assemble a thought, and the word then carries no summarising meaning at all. Worth recognising, not worth imitating.

One genuine risk: aiming `つまり` at what *somebody else* just said can sound like a correction - "so what you actually meant was…". A softener fixes it: つまり、こういうことでしょうか. Aimed at your own words it is completely safe, and in a presentation it is a useful signpost that the summary has arrived.

---

## つまり · Nuance & register (cont.)

`つまり` is not a cause-and-effect connector. `だから` and したがって say "therefore, here is a new fact"; `つまり` says "the same fact, re-expressed". When the second sentence contains information the first one did not, you want `だから`.

---

## つまり · つまり vs 要するに

> **Rule of thumb** - `つまり` re-expresses; <code><ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに</code> compresses. The second one claims the right to decide what the point was.

<ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わりました。**つまり**、<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>の<ruby>南口<rt>みなみぐち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>集合<rt>しゅうごう</rt></ruby>です。<br>*The venue has changed - that is, we meet at the south exit of the station.*

<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>長<rt>なが</rt></ruby>かったが、**<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに**<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>足<rt>た</rt></ruby>りないのだ。<br>*The explanation went on a while, but the gist is that there isn't enough budget.*

<code><ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに</code> implies the original was long-winded, so pointing it at a superior's remarks is risky. `つまり` carries no such judgement.

---

## つまり · つまり vs すなわち

> **Rule of thumb** - same job, different clothes. すなわち is the written, formal register: it puts an equals sign between two terms.

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>首都<rt>しゅと</rt></ruby>、**すなわち**<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>本社<rt>ほんしゃ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>置<rt>お</rt></ruby>いている。<br>*Our head office is in the capital of Japan, namely Tokyo.*

In conversation すなわち sounds like a legal document being read aloud. Reach for `つまり` when you are speaking, and keep すなわち for formal writing, where it is usually left in kana.

---

## つまり · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>っていた。つまり、<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>になった。 → ✅ <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>っていた。**だから**、<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>になった。<br>*The cancellation is a new event, not a restatement of the rain. `つまり` needs the second sentence to be the *same* content in another form.*

- ❌ つまり<ruby>三人<rt>さんにん</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ました。 → ✅ <ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>三人<rt>さんにん</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ました。<br>*`つまり` cannot introduce a plain new fact out of nowhere. Something has to have been said already for it to restate.*

- ❌ <ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに、<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>のおっしゃりたいことは…（said to your own teacher）→ ✅ **つまり**、<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>のおっしゃりたいことは…<br>*Summarising a superior's words with <code><ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに</code> hints that they rambled. `つまり` is the neutral choice whenever the words being restated are not your own.*

---

## つまり · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>木曜<rt>もくよう</rt></ruby>も<ruby>金曜<rt>きんよう</rt></ruby>も<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>っている。____、<ruby>今週<rt>こんしゅう</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。

{reveal}
**つまり**、<ruby>今週<rt>こんしゅう</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>がない。

{reveal}
The second sentence adds no new information - it is the first one seen from a step back. That is exactly the restating job, and `だから` would also be possible if you wanted to present it as a result rather than a rewording.

---

## つまり · Practice 2

**2.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>のお<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>減<rt>へ</rt></ruby>らせということですね。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>のお<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>は、**つまり**<ruby>予算<rt>よさん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>減<rt>へ</rt></ruby>らせということですね。

{reveal}
Grammatically the original is fine, but <code><ruby>要<rt>よう</rt></ruby>するに</code> tells your manager that his explanation needed boiling down. `つまり` restates without passing judgement on the length of the original.

---

## つまり · Practice 3

**3.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>会員<rt>かいいん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>無料<rt>むりょう</rt></ruby>です。つまり、お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>はかかりません。 (b) <ruby>会員<rt>かいいん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>無料<rt>むりょう</rt></ruby>です。だから、みんな<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>りたがります。

{reveal}
In (a) the two halves are the same fact twice, the second time in plainer words, so `つまり` is doing a translation job for the listener. In (b) the second half is a separate fact that follows from the first, which calls for a causal connector. The test is simple: if deleting the second clause loses no information at all, `つまり` is the word you want.

---

# たとえば

**Meaning** · for example; say - pulling one concrete case out of a general statement

`たとえば` warns the listener that what follows is an illustration, not a new claim. The example is offered as one of several possibilities, which is why it so often arrives with `とか` or `など` trailing behind it.

---

## たとえば · Usage

`たとえば` normally stands at the head of the sentence, but it can also sit directly in front of the noun phrase it is introducing:

- <ruby>果物<rt>くだもの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。たとえば、みかんとかぶどうとか。
- <ruby>近<rt>ちか</rt></ruby>くの<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>、たとえばコンビニでも<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>えます。

Three shapes carry most of its use:

---

## たとえば · Usage (cont.)

- **たとえば～とか／など** - a list left deliberately open.<br>*たとえば<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>のアプリなど、<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>えるものがいいです。*
- **たとえば～のような／みたいな + noun** - the example modifies a noun.<br>*たとえば<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>のような<ruby>古<rt>ふる</rt></ruby>い<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>*
- **たとえば～なら** - set up a hypothetical case and then say what happens in it.<br>*たとえば<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>なら、<ruby>中<rt>なか</rt></ruby>でやりましょう。*

In kanji it is <ruby>例<rt>たと</rt></ruby>えば, and both spellings are completely normal: printed prose and official documents tend to use the kanji, casual writing the kana. The reading and the meaning are identical either way.

---

## たとえば · Usage (cont.)

Do not confuse it with `たとえ`, which is a different word entirely - see the contrast below.

---

## たとえば · Examples

<ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>いものが<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。**たとえば**、チョコレートやアイスです。<br>*I like sweet things - chocolate and ice cream, for example.*

**たとえば**、この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>三<rt>みっ</rt></ruby>つあります。<br>*This kanji, for instance, has three different readings.*

<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みの<ruby>日<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>にできること、**たとえば**<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>とか<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>とかを<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>やしたい。<br>*I want more things I can do on a day off - walks, cooking, that sort of thing.*

**たとえば**<ruby>地震<rt>じしん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたら、まず<ruby>机<rt>つくえ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ってください。<br>*Say an earthquake happens - the first thing to do is get under a desk.*

---

## たとえば · Nuance & register

Register-neutral. Nothing about `たとえば` marks formality, age or gender, and it appears unchanged in academic writing and in chat with friends.

Two conversational uses are worth memorising whole. 「たとえばの<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>だけど」 prefaces a hypothetical you are not committing to - "just supposing, though". And 「たとえば?」 said alone is a request for one: "such as?" That one-word question is enormously useful and very common.

In writing, a `たとえば` sentence is usually short and ends with `など`, `といった` or a plain noun phrase, and the paragraph then returns to the general point. If you find yourself giving three sentences of example, consider <ruby>具体<rt>ぐたい</rt></ruby><ruby>的<rt>てき</rt></ruby>には ("specifically") instead, which promises a fuller account.

---

## たとえば · Nuance & register (cont.)

`たとえば` presents one member of a set. When you want to say that your example is the *representative* one - the first of many, the flagship - Japanese has `をはじめ` for that, and it is not interchangeable.

---

## たとえば · たとえば vs たとえ○○ても

> **Rule of thumb** - `たとえば` introduces an example. `たとえ` introduces a concession, and it always has a `ても` waiting for it later in the sentence.

**たとえば**<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ったら、どうしますか。<br>*If it rains tomorrow, say, what will you do?*

**たとえ**<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>っ**ても**、<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>はやります。<br>*Even if it rains tomorrow, the match is going ahead.*

The first sentence asks about one possible case among many; the second brushes the case aside. The `ば` is the whole difference in writing, and in speech the giveaway is the `ても` at the far end: if you hear one, the word at the front was `たとえ`.

---

## たとえば · Common mistakes

- ❌ たとえ<ruby>日本料理<rt>にほんりょうり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。 → ✅ **たとえば**<ruby>日本料理<rt>にほんりょうり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。<br>*Without the `ば` the word means "even if", and the sentence is left dangling with nothing for it to concede to.*

- ❌ たとえば、<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人口<rt>じんこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>約<rt>やく</rt></ruby><ruby>一億<rt>いちおく</rt></ruby><ruby>二千万人<rt>にせんまんにん</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人口<rt>じんこう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>約<rt>やく</rt></ruby><ruby>一億<rt>いちおく</rt></ruby><ruby>二千万人<rt>にせんまんにん</rt></ruby>です。<br>*A single hard fact is not an example of anything. `たとえば` needs a general statement in front of it for the example to illustrate.*

- ❌ <ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>、たとえばにんじんをはじめ<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。 → ✅ <ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>、**たとえば**にんじんなどを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。<br>*`たとえば` pairs with `など`, `とか` and `といった`. `をはじめ` is a different pattern meaning "starting with", and the two cannot be stacked.*

---

## たとえば · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby><ruby>不足<rt>ぶそく</rt></ruby>なので、____<ruby>階段<rt>かいだん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>うようにしています。

{reveal}
**たとえば**<ruby>階段<rt>かいだん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>うようにしています。

{reveal}
The stairs are one concrete instance of the general problem stated first, which is what this word is for. Note that the example still needs the general statement in front of it to lean on.

---

## たとえば · Practice 2

**2.** Choose the right word: （たとえ・たとえば）<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>しても、やってみる<ruby>価値<rt>かち</rt></ruby>はある。

{reveal}
**たとえ**<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>しても、やってみる<ruby>価値<rt>かち</rt></ruby>はある。

{reveal}
The `ても` later in the sentence is the tell: this is a concession, "even if I fail", not an illustration. `たとえば` would leave the `ても` with no partner.

---

## たとえば · Practice 3

**3.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かな<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>、たとえば<ruby>奈良<rt>なら</rt></ruby>のような<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>みたい。 (b) <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かな<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>、<ruby>奈良<rt>なら</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>みたい。

{reveal}
Sentence (a) uses Nara as an illustration of the kind of town the speaker wants; other quiet towns would do just as well, and nobody would be surprised if they ended up somewhere else. Sentence (b) names Nara as the actual destination and describes it as quiet along the way. The example frame is what keeps the choice open.

---

# 確かに

**Meaning** · certainly; admittedly; you're right - vouching for something, or granting a point before you argue with it

<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに has two lives. It can mean "definitely, without doubt", said of something you are sure of. Far more often at this level it means "granted" - you concede what the other person said, and then the `が` or `けど` arrives.

---

## 確かに · Usage

<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに is an adverb: it goes in front of the predicate, or at the head of the sentence, and never changes shape. Three uses:

- **Conceding** - the big one. <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに～が／けど、～. The first half agrees,<br>*the second half pushes back. <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いが、<ruby>質<rt>しつ</rt></ruby>はいい。*
- **Vouching** - "for certain", of an event you witnessed or a fact you can stand<br>*behind. <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>渡<rt>わた</rt></ruby>しました。*
- **Agreeing, on its own** - 「<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに。」 is a complete turn in<br>*conversation, meaning "true" or "fair point". This is very common in modern casual speech.*

---

## 確かに · Usage (cont.)

The single most useful thing to remember is the concessive frame. Whenever an essay or a discussion needs "it's true that…, but…", <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに at the front and `が` in the middle is the standard shape, and a listener hears the `が` coming the moment you say the first word.

Kanji <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに and kana たしかに are both normal; the kanji is the default in print.

---

## 確かに · Examples

「この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いね。」「**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**。」<br>*"This place is cheap." "It is, isn't it."*

**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>いけど、<ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>らないよ。<br>*It's cold, admittedly, but it isn't going to snow.*

<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**お<ruby>預<rt>あず</rt></ruby>かりしました。<br>*I have received the documents - they are safely with me.*

**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりやすかったが、<ruby>肝心<rt>かんじん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>費用<rt>ひよう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>抜<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>けていた。<br>*His explanation was certainly easy to follow, but it left out the crucial question of cost.*

---

## 確かに · Nuance & register

Register-neutral, and equally at home in an academic paper and in a text message. The concessive frame <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに～が is a staple of written argument; the one-word 「<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに。」 reply is casual but not slangy, and works in the office as well as with friends.

The vouching use has a slightly formal flavour, because it is what you say when responsibility is at stake: <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>承<rt>うけたまわ</rt></ruby>りました, "I have definitely taken note of that", is standard business phrasing. In everyday talk about the future, きっと is the natural word instead.

---

## 確かに · Nuance & register (cont.)

Be aware of what conceding does to the shape of a conversation. Opening with <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに sets up an expectation that a `が` is coming; if you concede and then stop, the listener will wait for the rest of the sentence. That is often exactly the effect you want when disagreeing politely - the agreement takes the sting out of what follows - but it does mean <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに is rarely the whole of your position.

---

## 確かに · 確かに vs 確か

> **Rule of thumb** - one `に` reverses the meaning. <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに is confidence; <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か is a memory you are not sure of.

**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か**<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>からだったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。<br>*The meeting was at three, if I remember rightly.*

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**<ruby>三時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まりました。<br>*The meeting definitely started at three.*

---

## 確かに · 確かに vs 確か (cont.)

<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か is an adverb of *hedged recollection* and normally comes with と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う, はず or だったよね. <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに asserts. Mixing them up tells your listener the opposite of what you meant, which is why this pair is worth drilling.

---

## 確かに · 確かに vs きっと

> **Rule of thumb** - <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに is about what is already established. きっと is a confident guess about what is not.

<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>は**きっと**<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ます。<br>*She'll definitely come.*

<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ました。<br>*She did come - I can vouch for it.*

きっと looks forward and is a prediction, however confident; <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに looks back at evidence. Saying ❌<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ます about a future event sounds like you are promising on someone else's behalf.

---

## 確かに · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でしょう。 → ✅ **きっと**<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でしょう。<br>*A forecast is a guess, not something you can vouch for. <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに needs evidence already in hand.*

- ❌ <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんの<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>だったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。 → ✅ **<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か**<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんの<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>だったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。<br>*と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います signals that you are not sure, so the hedging <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か is the form that fits. With `に` the sentence contradicts itself.*

- ❌ <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かにです。 → ✅ **<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**そうですね。<br>*<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに is an adverb and cannot take `です` directly. To agree politely, give it something to modify.*

---

## 確かに · Practice 1

**1.** ____<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>な<ruby>場所<rt>ばしょ</rt></ruby>だが、<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いのは<ruby>魅力<rt>みりょく</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに**<ruby>不便<rt>ふべん</rt></ruby>な<ruby>場所<rt>ばしょ</rt></ruby>だが、<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いのは<ruby>魅力<rt>みりょく</rt></ruby>だ。

{reveal}
The `が` in the middle is the giveaway: the writer grants the drawback first and then argues past it, which is the standard concessive frame this word builds.

---

## 確かに · Practice 2

**2.** Choose the right form: （<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か・<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かに）<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たはずです。

{reveal}
**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>か**<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>も<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たはずです。

{reveal}
`はず` marks this as inference from a hazy memory rather than a fact the speaker can guarantee, so the hedging form without `に` is the one that fits.

---

## 確かに · Practice 3

**3.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かにこの<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>い。 (b) この<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>速<rt>はや</rt></ruby>い。

{reveal}
Sentence (b) is a flat statement of the speaker's own view. Sentence (a) sounds like a reply: it accepts a point somebody else has made, and it leaves the door open for a "but" - about cost, or safety, or whatever the speaker is really driving at. Ending there without the "but" makes the agreement sound reluctant.

---

# おそらく

**Meaning** · in all likelihood; probably - a considered estimate, stated carefully

`おそらく` is the measured, slightly formal cousin of たぶん. It says the speaker has weighed what they know and arrived at a probable answer. The weighing is the point: `おそらく` sounds like a judgement, not a shrug.

---

## おそらく · Usage

`おそらく` is an adverb and stands at the head of the sentence or immediately before the predicate. It never conjugates and takes no particles.

What matters is the **end of the sentence**. `おそらく` almost always pairs with a marker of conjecture:

- **おそらく～だろう／でしょう** - the default.<br>*おそらく<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>には<ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>くでしょう。*
- **おそらく～と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う／と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われる** - reasoning out loud, or in<br>*writing. おそらく<ruby>原因<rt>げんいん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>配線<rt>はいせん</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われます。*
- **おそらく～はずだ／に<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない** - when the estimate is close to a<br>*conclusion. おそらく<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いているはずだ。*

---

## おそらく · Usage (cont.)

Ending a plain assertion with nothing at all - ❌おそらく<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る - sounds unfinished to a native ear. The hedge at the end is not decoration; it is what `おそらく` is agreeing with.

In kanji it is <ruby>恐<rt>おそ</rt></ruby>らく. The kanji spelling is common in print; the kana is common in ordinary writing. It has nothing to do with fear despite the character.

---

## おそらく · Examples

**おそらく**<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っているでしょう。<br>*He probably already knows.*

この<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>なら、**おそらく**<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>空<rt>す</rt></ruby>いているだろう。<br>*At this hour the roads are most likely clear.*

<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>がないところを<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ると、**おそらく**<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいのだろう。<br>*Judging by the lack of a reply, he's probably swamped.*

<ruby>今回<rt>こんかい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>不具合<rt>ふぐあい</rt></ruby>は、**おそらく**<ruby>先月<rt>せんげつ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>更新<rt>こうしん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>原因<rt>げんいん</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えられます。<br>*This fault is in all likelihood caused by last month's update.*

---

## おそらく · Nuance & register

`おそらく` leans formal. It is the natural choice in a report, a news article, a presentation or a careful explanation to a client, and it sounds a little stiff between friends deciding where to eat, where たぶん is what people actually say.

It also leans toward **inference about circumstances** rather than announcements about your own plans. たぶん<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます ("I'll probably go") is ordinary; おそらく<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます sounds oddly detached, as though you were forecasting the behaviour of a stranger who happens to be you. Reserve `おそらく` for things outside your control.

On the confidence scale, `おそらく` sits high - above もしかしたら, roughly level with or a shade above たぶん - but it is still a guess. If you know, say so plainly; hedging a fact with `おそらく` reads as evasive, and in business that impression is hard to shake off.

---

## おそらく · おそらく vs たぶん

> **Rule of thumb** - same probability, different room. `たぶん` is spoken and casual; `おそらく` is written and considered.

**たぶん**<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>うと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うよ。<br>*We'll probably make it, I reckon.*

**おそらく**<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>うものと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われます。<br>*We are likely to arrive in time.*

`たぶん` can be tossed off with no evidence at all; `おそらく` implies you looked at something first. In casual conversation `おそらく` is not wrong, merely bookish.

---

## おそらく · おそらく vs きっと

> **Rule of thumb** - `おそらく` estimates. `きっと` believes.

**きっと**<ruby>喜<rt>よろこ</rt></ruby>んでくれるよ。<br>*She's going to love it.*

**おそらく**<ruby>喜<rt>よろこ</rt></ruby>んでくれるだろう。<br>*She will probably be pleased.*

`きっと` carries the speaker's feeling - hope, conviction, encouragement - and is what you say when reassuring someone. `おそらく` carries none of that warmth, which makes it excellent for analysis and poor for comfort.

---

## おそらく · Common mistakes

- ❌ おそらく<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ります。 → ✅ おそらく<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る**でしょう**。<br>*A flat ます-ending states a fact, which contradicts the word at the front. `おそらく` needs `でしょう`, `だろう` or と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います to lean on.*

- ❌ おそらく<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>りました。 → ✅ **たぶん**<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。<br>*You do not estimate your own past actions from the outside. `おそらく` is for inference about things you did not do.*

- ❌ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>のパーティー、おそらく<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くね。 → ✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>のパーティー、**たぶん**<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くね。<br>*Announcing your own plans to a friend calls for the casual word. `おそらく` with the final particle `ね` mixes two registers in one short sentence.*

---

## おそらく · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>電気<rt>でんき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>消<rt>き</rt></ruby>えているから、____もう<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ているだろう。

{reveal}
**おそらく**もう<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ているだろう。

{reveal}
The speaker reasons from visible evidence - the lights are off - to a probable conclusion, and the `だろう` at the end is the partner this adverb expects.

---

## おそらく · Practice 2

**2.** Choose the natural word: この<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>は、（きっと・おそらく）<ruby>気温<rt>きおん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>によるものと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われる。

{reveal}
**おそらく**<ruby>気温<rt>きおん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>影響<rt>えいきょう</rt></ruby>によるものと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われる。

{reveal}
The sentence is written analysis, complete with the formal と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われる ending. `きっと` would import a note of personal conviction that does not belong in a report.

---

## おそらく · Practice 3

**3.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) おそらく<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないでしょう。 (b) もしかしたら<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないかもしれません。

{reveal}
